header.subject: NPD
header.professor: Diptiprakash Pradhan (Modules 1-7); Prof. Ganesh Prabhu (Module 8 recap)
header.exam_format: 2 sections - Sec A (30 MCQ, 1 mark each), Sec B (9 short answer, 5 marks each). No negative marking. 120 min.
header.style_profile: NO CLA EXISTS for NPD (Section 4), so style is INFERRED from the module transcripts + the known exam format and difficulty is calibrated CONSERVATIVELY (closer to Easy/Normal) until the student corrects it. The course is a process/framework course taught around the NPD funnel (PIC/charter -> idea generation -> concept testing -> design/prototyping -> product-use testing -> market testing -> launch) and is heavily example-driven (Lego, Gillette Mach3, Rubbermaid, Chipotle, CarryPro, Luxottica, Southwest, IPL, iPhone, Nokia/AMD, Swatch/Shimano, Pixar). Sec A (1-mark MCQs) are best framed as definition/classification/'which-framework' or 'which-category' items (e.g. identify a Kano category, a modularity type, a PSS type, an adopter category, a legal basis for liability, horizontal vs vertical differentiation) plus a few light calculations (ATAR multiplicative demand; QFD weighting with 9/3/1 relationship scores). Sec B (5-mark short answers) ask to DEFINE/EXPLAIN a framework, APPLY it to a short scenario, COMPARE two concepts (modular vs integral, red vs blue ocean, alpha vs beta vs gamma, internal vs external integrity, product- vs use- vs result-oriented PSS), or LIST-and-explain (steps/types/benefits). Distractors should be ADJACENT frameworks or the reversed pole of a dichotomy - the core trap is funnel-stage/framework confusion and reversed dichotomies (e.g. integral<->modular, horizontal<->vertical, alpha<->beta, who-owns in PSS, eliminate/reduce vs raise/create). ALWAYS establish the funnel stage in the scenario before asking a stage-dependent question (Section 4 failure mode: funnel-dependency skipping).
header.no_cla_note: Per Section 4 and the CLA filename map (Section 6), NPD has no CLA file. Module _merged_module.txt files were the SOLE source. Per-chapter .txt files on disk are all 0 bytes (empty), so per Section 6 ('read per-chapter files, plus _merged_module.txt only if per-chapter files are absent') the merged module files are the valid source. Difficulty defaults to 1-2 (Easy/Normal); only the two calculation nodes (ATAR, QFD weighting) are set to 3, to be re-calibrated by the student via play.
header.stage_in_funnel_tagging: Section 4 requires stage_in_funnel on every node. Canonical funnel (Section 4): PIC -> Idea Generation -> Concept Testing -> Prototyping -> Market Testing -> Launch. Two documented extensions are used: 'Product Use Testing' (alpha/beta/gamma and test designs, which sit between Prototyping and Market Testing per Module 4) and 'Cross-Cutting' (Module 5 strategy interface, IP, emerging markets, design thinking, soft innovation and practitioner cases that genuinely span every stage). context_tag carries the finer thematic grouping (foundations/business_model/process/portfolio/idea_generation/market_research/concept_testing/evaluation/calculation/design/prototyping/organization/services/testing/demand_creation/ip/blue_ocean/business_plan/emerging_markets/design_thinking/soft_innovation/launch/market_testing/policy/case).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Firms need new products to sustain competitive advantage: competitors copy and catch up, eroding any edge, so a firm must keep offering something better or cheaper (product differentiation or cost leadership). Without continuous new products a firm loses the ability to make customers prefer it and to charge a price above cost. New products are also driven by changing technology, customer tastes and competitive pressure.

distractors.wrong: New products exist mainly to use up R&D budgets
distractors.why: the driver is sustaining competitive advantage and preventing imitation from eroding margins, not spending budget

distractors.wrong: A firm with a market-leading product never needs new ones
distractors.why: complacency kills leaders (Kodak, Nokia); competitors catch up and the advantage decays

nodes.sample_question: Explain why continuous new product development is necessary for a firm even when its current product is a market leader. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating NPD as optional rather than as the engine that renews competitive advantage.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: New products span a spectrum of novelty: (1) new-to-the-world (breakthrough, creates a new market, e.g. first iPhone/laser printer); (2) new product line for the firm (entering a new business, e.g. P&G's first shampoo, Canon's first printer); (3) line extensions / additions to existing line (e.g. new Pepsi flavour); (4) improvements/revisions of existing products (small tweaks, new variant); (5) repositioning (same product, new use/segment, e.g. aspirin as heart treatment); (6) cost reductions (same benefit at lower cost, e.g. plastic replacing steel parts). Novelty decreases and risk/innovation intensity decreases across the list.

distractors.wrong: A line extension is the same as a new-to-the-world product
distractors.why: line extensions reuse an existing line; new-to-world creates a new market and carries far higher novelty/risk

distractors.wrong: Repositioning requires changing the physical product
distractors.why: repositioning changes the target/use/branding for the same product, e.g. aspirin repositioned for heart attacks

nodes.sample_question: Aspirin, long sold as a painkiller, is marketed as a daily heart-attack preventative with no change to the pill. Which new-product category is this? (1M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing repositioning (marketing change) with a genuine new-line or improvement (product change).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Innovation underpins every new product and comes in three levels: (1) discontinuous/disruptive (radical) innovation — breakthrough, new technology, creates new markets; (2) architectural innovation — improvements to process, features or technology for mid-range products; (3) incremental innovation — slight feature changes, line extensions, cost reduction, repositioning. Continuous innovation prevents commoditisation/stagnation and protects margins.

distractors.wrong: All innovation must be radical/breakthrough to count
distractors.why: most innovation is incremental or architectural; continuous small innovation protects margins and is the bulk of NPD

distractors.wrong: Incremental innovation and cost reduction are the same as a new market
distractors.why: incremental sits at the low-novelty end; only discontinuous/radical innovation creates a new market

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish discontinuous (radical), architectural, and incremental innovation, giving one example of each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating 'innovation' only with radical breakthroughs and ignoring architectural/incremental innovation.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The product manager has end-to-end ownership of a product's success and is a general-management (not specialist) role: balancing marketing, finance, operations and strategy across the whole development process. The role combines creativity (positioning, selection) with risk-taking, because roughly half of new products fail. A great idea alone is not enough — it must fit customer requirement, organisational capability and feasible cost at a price customers will pay. Large organisations therefore use a structured step-by-step process rather than 'ready-fire-aim'.

distractors.wrong: The product manager is a functional specialist in marketing
distractors.why: it is a multifunctional general-management role spanning marketing, finance, operations and strategy

distractors.wrong: A great idea is sufficient for product success
distractors.why: the idea must also fit customer need, firm capability and feasible cost; structure and execution matter more

nodes.sample_question: Why is the product manager described as a general-management rather than a functional-specialist role? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing the product manager to a marketing specialist and ignoring the cross-functional, risk-taking nature.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: New product development is inherently multidisciplinary, integrating strategy (generic strategy, industry structure), design (creative design thinking), marketing (product, pricing) and operations, from idea generation through to launch. The objective can be commercial or social value creation. Understanding strategy first is the foundation; design, marketing and operations then combine to make new products efficient and effective.

distractors.wrong: NPD is essentially a marketing activity
distractors.why: it integrates strategy, design, marketing AND operations — marketing is only one discipline

distractors.wrong: NPD only creates commercial products
distractors.why: the objective can also be social value creation, not just commercial products

nodes.sample_question: List the disciplines that NPD integrates and explain why it is called a multidisciplinary process. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Seeing NPD through a single functional lens instead of as cross-disciplinary integration.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A product-centric view focuses on what the firm is excited to build; a user-centric view focuses on what value the user perceives. The BottleLoft case (magnetic strip that lifts bottles to the fridge roof) shows the trap: the 'STRONG LIKE BULL' campaign over-emphasised magnet strength while ignoring the high-bond 3M adhesive that actually holds the strip — creating customer dissonance. User-centric development resolves such dissonances by communicating what the user actually worries about. Feature vs cost is also not linear: adding features early in development is cheap; adding them late is far costlier.

distractors.wrong: Product-centric and user-centric views always agree
distractors.why: they can diverge: the firm's pride (strong magnet) ignored the user's real concern (will the adhesive hold?)

distractors.wrong: Adding features late in development costs about the same as early
distractors.why: late changes cost ~10-100x more; the feature-cost relationship is non-linear and timing-dependent

nodes.sample_question: Using the BottleLoft 'STRONG LIKE BULL' case, contrast product-centric and user-centric views and explain the dissonance created. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Designing/communicating from the firm's pride in the product rather than the user's actual perceived value.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A business model answers who is the customer, what do they value, how does the firm make money, and can it deliver value at reasonable cost. It must pass two tests: the NARRATIVE test (a coherent story of the customer — who/what/why/how much they pay) and the NUMBERS test (value vs cost, projected profits add up). New products often fail because of an inappropriate business model; existing models fail when the assumptions/limits they were built on get stretched too far and projected returns don't materialise. A robust model survives when limits are stretched and signals the need for corrective action.

distractors.wrong: A business model is just a pricing or marketing tactic
distractors.why: it re-architects who the customer is and how value is created/captured, not a one-off tactic

distractors.wrong: A model passes if it tells a good story
distractors.why: it must pass BOTH the narrative test and the numbers test (value vs cost / profit)

nodes.sample_question: State the two tests every new-product business model must pass and explain what each checks. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Checking the story (narrative) but never the numbers, or treating the model as mere pricing.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Uber's model solves the taxi 'discovery' problem: it aggregates drivers and riders, confirms rides fast, reduces drivers' empty (dry-run) time, and prices dynamically by demand/supply (surge). It CREATES value (efficiency, fast availability, fairness across stakeholders) — that is the business model. Capturing that value against competitors is business STRATEGY: a model is opportunity-centric (creating value by exploiting user context) while strategy is competition-centric (advantage over rivals). Surge pricing raises availability during shortages rather than overcharging.

distractors.wrong: Surge pricing is simply overcharging during shortages
distractors.why: higher price pulls more drivers onto the road, raising car availability — it allocates scarce supply, not pure overcharging

distractors.wrong: Business model and business strategy are the same thing
distractors.why: the model creates value (opportunity-centric); strategy captures it against rivals (competition-centric)

nodes.sample_question: Using Uber, distinguish 'creating value' (business model) from 'capturing value' (business strategy). (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Conflating value creation (model) with value capture (strategy), and reading surge pricing as mere gouging.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The NPD process runs PIC/charter -> idea generation -> concept generation & evaluation -> product design/development -> prototype & testing -> launch -> post-launch service. Crucially the stages are NOT strictly sequential — they are fluid and overlapping (e.g. marketing and service-network planning begin before the product is finished). The process refines a product from many ideas down to a launched product.

distractors.wrong: The NPD stages must run strictly one after another
distractors.why: stages are fluid and overlapping; marketing/service planning can start before development finishes

distractors.wrong: Post-launch service is outside the NPD process
distractors.why: service network setup and post-launch support are part of the end-to-end process

nodes.sample_question: Outline the stages of the NPD process and explain why they are described as fluid and overlapping rather than sequential. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating NPD as a rigid linear waterfall instead of overlapping stages.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The Product Innovation Charter is the strategy document for new products: it states the product's purpose in line with the firm's objectives — new design, market positioning (premium vs mass), and financial objectives (e.g. target market share or profit by a date). The PIC gives clarity that makes execution possible; without it, execution becomes tentative. It is part of the mission statement and keeps every stage aligned to the firm's goals.

distractors.wrong: The PIC is a detailed engineering specification
distractors.why: the PIC is a strategic charter (purpose, positioning, financial goals), not component-level specs

distractors.wrong: A PIC is optional once ideas start flowing
distractors.why: without a charter execution becomes tentative; it is the strategic anchor revisited at each stage

nodes.sample_question: What is a Product Innovation Charter and what must it specify? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the strategic charter (purpose/positioning/financial goals) with a technical spec.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.concept: Mission statement for a new product
nodes.teaching_note: A new-product mission statement specifies: product description; key business goals (launch timing, gross-margin and market-share targets by a date); primary market and secondary market(s); explicit assumptions ('givens', e.g. solar-powered, sealed/waterproof, child-safe with no small parts); and stakeholders (children/users, parents, teachers, retailers, sales force, production/QC, environment, servicing). The kids' calculator example illustrates each element.

distractors.wrong: The mission statement only names the target customer
distractors.why: it also covers business goals, secondary markets, explicit assumptions/'givens' and all stakeholders

distractors.wrong: Assumptions ('givens') need not be written down
distractors.why: writing assumptions (solar power, sealed, child-safe) prevents downstream design conflicts

nodes.sample_question: Using the kids'-calculator example, list the elements a new-product mission statement should contain. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Listing only the primary market and omitting goals, assumptions and the full stakeholder set.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A firm balances a portfolio along a commitment spectrum: SUPPORT products (minimal/incremental change to existing line, give immediate cash flow), DERIVATIVE products (small changes derived from a base, e.g. Swift -> Baleno), PLATFORM products (next-generation, new benefits on a shared base, medium-term), and BREAKTHROUGH products (radical new core technology, long-term). Map them to time horizons: support = short term, platform = medium (2-5 yrs), breakthrough = long term. Over-relying on either extreme is dangerous — only support means no future; only breakthrough means insufficient cash flow.

distractors.wrong: Derivative and breakthrough products require the same commitment
distractors.why: they sit at opposite ends: derivatives are small base-changes; breakthroughs are radical new core technology

distractors.wrong: A firm should focus only on breakthrough products
distractors.why: without support/derivative cash flow it cannot fund the 3-5 year breakthrough cycle; balance is required

nodes.sample_question: Place support, derivative, platform and breakthrough products on a commitment/time-horizon spectrum and explain why a balanced portfolio is needed. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the portfolio as one product type instead of a balanced mix across horizons.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A balanced portfolio is mapped on two dimensions: extent of ENABLING TECHNOLOGY change (basic -> new/radical) and extent of CUSTOMER-NEED change (met by current product -> new need). Projects spread across the diagonal: small innovations/re-branding at the low-low corner, radical breakthroughs at the high-high corner, with derivative and platform projects in between. A lopsided portfolio (only breakthroughs) undervalues current products; (only current products) means no future once competition catches up.

distractors.wrong: Portfolio balance is measured only by number of products
distractors.why: it is mapped on technology-change and customer-need-change dimensions, not a simple count

distractors.wrong: Working only on current-product improvements is a safe balanced strategy
distractors.why: it leaves no breakthrough pipeline, so there is no market position once competition matures

nodes.sample_question: On which two dimensions is a balanced product portfolio mapped, and what is the danger of a lopsided portfolio? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring the technology-vs-need framing and the risk of a lopsided pipeline.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.concept: Portfolio decisions for a new product
nodes.teaching_note: When adding a new product, decide across dimensions relative to the existing line: BRAND (same brand to leverage trust, or different brand to avoid devaluing existing quality); MARKET (same customers/use occasion or different); PRICING (premium justified, or cost-effective); COST (controllable via shared resources?); OPERATIONS (shared supply chain/plant?); DISTRIBUTION (same dealer network/channel?); accessories & service; product-level vs component-level vs service-level competition. Deciding these early avoids costly late discovery; cannibalisation must be managed.

distractors.wrong: A new product should always reuse the parent brand
distractors.why: same brand only if comparable quality; a lower-quality product under the parent brand devalues it

distractors.wrong: Portfolio decisions can be deferred until after launch
distractors.why: deciding brand/price/channel/cost late causes costly rework and derailment; decide early

nodes.sample_question: List five dimensions a firm must decide on when adding a new product to its portfolio. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting brand-devaluation and cannibalisation risks when extending a line.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The development funnel starts WIDE (many customer needs combined with many technological possibilities -> many concepts) and progressively NARROWS through concept generation -> concept selection -> product design -> development/prototype -> testing -> launch. Keep maximum flexibility early and make commitments later. A funnel too wide wastes energy on irrelevant options; too narrow starves the process of good ideas. The right width depends on the business.

distractors.wrong: The funnel should be as narrow as possible from the start
distractors.why: early stages need a WIDE funnel for flexibility; narrowing too early starves the process of good options

distractors.wrong: Concept selection comes before concept generation
distractors.why: the order is generation (wide) then selection (narrowing); you cannot select before generating

nodes.sample_question: Explain the product development funnel and why maximum flexibility belongs early rather than late. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Narrowing the funnel too early and locking into concepts before enough are generated.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Stage gates are go/no-go checkpoints placed on the funnel where management decides whether a project proceeds or is dropped, so limited resources back only viable projects. A typical gate sequence: Gate 1 idea generation/initial screening -> Gate 2 feasibility check (customer relevance, technical & commercial issues) -> Gate 3 business capability (proven technology, commercial viability) -> Gate 4 launch preparation. Effective management requires: clear communication of the process, transparent assessment criteria at each gate, top-management commitment, periodic review against agreed standards, good documentation, and cross-functional teams. You CANNOT manage stage gates without first establishing the funnel structure.

distractors.wrong: A stage gate is just a project status meeting
distractors.why: it is an explicit go/no-go decision that can kill a project to protect resources, with defined criteria

distractors.wrong: Dropping projects without stated criteria is fine
distractors.why: opaque drops demotivate employees; criteria must be transparent and communicated

nodes.sample_question: What is a stage gate, and list four requirements for managing stage gates effectively. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Discussing stage gates without first establishing the funnel they sit on (funnel-dependency skipping).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Because markets and technology are uncertain and development can take years, building in flexibility lets late design changes happen at lower cost — but flexibility has a downside (can lead to poorer-quality products if discipline slips, and late flexibility itself costs more). Manage the economic trade-off: adopt flexible/fast low-cost design iteration technologies, structure tasks for progressive commitment, lock down requirements while keeping backup options, and use MODULAR product structures to decouple parts so some can change while others stay fixed. Not all projects can be flexible.

distractors.wrong: More flexibility is always better
distractors.why: flexibility trades off against cost and quality risk; you choose the best flexible approach via cost-benefit

distractors.wrong: Flexibility means leaving all requirements open
distractors.why: you lock down requirements progressively and keep targeted backups; total openness raises cost and quality risk

nodes.sample_question: Why is flexibility valuable in product development, and what is its main trade-off? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming flexibility is free upside rather than an economic trade-off against cost and quality.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Three core NPD process metrics: (1) LEAD TIME to market — time from idea generation to launch (shrinking across decades: Honda 5yr->3yr, HP printer years->months); (2) CAPACITY — number of products developed per unit time / launched per year; (3) PRODUCTIVITY — products developed per unit of effort or budget (e.g. per team-hours/years). These measure how innovative and efficient the organisation is at NPD.

distractors.wrong: Market share is one of the three core NPD development metrics
distractors.why: the three are lead time, capacity and productivity; market share is a performance/outcome metric, not a development-process metric

distractors.wrong: Lead time and productivity measure the same thing
distractors.why: lead time = speed to market; productivity = output per unit of effort/budget — distinct measures

nodes.sample_question: Name and define the three core product development process metrics. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Mixing financial/outcome metrics with the three process metrics (lead time, capacity, productivity).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Sources for new product opportunities: (1) changes in user LIFESTYLES & DEMOGRAPHY (e.g. health-conscious Gen Z); (2) studying COMPETITOR products for gaps/features; (3) SUGGESTIONS & feedback from existing users; (4) user FRUSTRATIONS with existing products (a strong signal); (5) innovations of LEAD USERS; (6) tracking emerging TECHNOLOGIES (ideas not viable today may become viable); (7) blank spaces on the BUYER UTILITY MAP. Maintain high-quality documentation of ideas (even dropped ones) to revisit later.

distractors.wrong: New product ideas come only from R&D/internal teams
distractors.why: ideas come from many external sources: lifestyle shifts, competitors, user frustrations, lead users, emerging tech, utility-map gaps

distractors.wrong: Dropped ideas should be discarded
distractors.why: keep documentation of dropped ideas — they may become viable later as technology/markets change

nodes.sample_question: List five distinct sources a firm can use to identify new product opportunities. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating opportunity identification as purely internal/R&D-driven.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Lego (founded 1932) neared bankruptcy by the late 1990s/2000s: complacency, a CEO who stopped listening to customers, lost touch with the kid community, and the digital onslaught (PlayStation). Revival came from acknowledging the problem, investing in product development and retail partners, running kid focus groups, and re-anchoring on the core purpose (joy of building). Lego embraced digital as a friend (Lego Ideas co-creation, My Own Creation), built adult super-fan communities and content creators, and forged partnerships (Star Wars, Harry Potter, Legoland), reviving revenue to ~$10bn. Lesson: complacency kills (Kodak, Xerox, Nokia); listen to customers, engage community, treat technology as a friend.

distractors.wrong: Lego's decline was caused mainly by poor manufacturing
distractors.why: the cause was complacency and losing touch with the customer community plus digital competition, not factory issues

distractors.wrong: Brand communities are irrelevant to product turnaround
distractors.why: community co-creation (Lego Ideas, super-fans, content creators) was central to the revival

nodes.sample_question: What caused Lego's near-bankruptcy and which actions drove its revival? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Attributing the turnaround to a single tactic rather than community engagement + refocusing on core purpose.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The Buyer Utility Map has two axes: horizontal = six STAGES of the customer experience cycle (purchase, delivery, use, supplements, maintenance, disposal); vertical = six UTILITY levers (customer productivity, simplicity, convenience, risk, fun/image, environmental friendliness). That gives 36 cells. Plot your offerings and competitors' across the cells: cells where you and competitors both compete are RED (overloaded, hard to win); empty cells are BLUE (unmet need, freedom to price and operate). Blue spaces reveal new product opportunities.

distractors.wrong: The Buyer Utility Map has stages on both axes
distractors.why: one axis is the six experience stages, the OTHER is the six utility levers (36 cells total)

distractors.wrong: Red (crowded) cells are the best opportunities
distractors.why: red cells are bleeding/competitive; BLUE empty cells are the opportunities with pricing freedom

nodes.sample_question: Describe the two axes of the Buyer Utility Map and explain the difference between red and blue cells. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Hunting in red (contested) cells instead of blue (empty) cells; mislabelling the two axes.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Frustrations reveal opportunities and fall into two groups. USER-side: the user doesn't know how to use the product, knows but can't use it, or finds it difficult/irritating to use. DESIGN-side (designer's fault): inappropriate design, product doesn't last as long as expected, it disturbs/affects other products used with it, wrong size/shape, or it fails to meet a special-needs segment. Observing frustrations -> remove them -> a superior product. A class exercise: list product, problem, nature of problem.

distractors.wrong: All product frustrations are the user's fault
distractors.why: frustrations split into user-side AND design-side (durability, size/shape, interference, special needs)

distractors.wrong: Frustration is a reason to abandon a category
distractors.why: frustration is an idea SOURCE — removing it yields a superior product, not a reason to exit

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish user-side from design-side product frustrations, with an example of each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Lumping all frustrations as user error and missing design-side failures.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Lead users have needs AHEAD of the market and a strong incentive to experiment because they face problems before ordinary users. Three types: (1) in the TARGET APPLICATION AREA (heavy/professional users of the product, e.g. barbers/tailors with scissors); (2) in an ANALOGOUS MARKET (similar application/different product, e.g. hedge cutters' notch idea borrowed for scissors); (3) SPECIALISTS in a problem area of the target product (e.g. book-publishing blade specialists for sharpness). Lead users give richer insight that helps refine products for ordinary users; the ICICI Bank/Finacle example shows a large lead-user client revealing real implementation complexity.

distractors.wrong: Lead users are simply early adopters
distractors.why: lead users have needs ahead of the market and experiment to solve them; early adopters merely buy early

distractors.wrong: Lead-user research replaces traditional market research
distractors.why: it COMPLEMENTS large-sample market research; lead-user samples are small and not the common user

nodes.sample_question: Define a lead user and describe the three types, with an example of each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating lead users with early adopters, or treating lead-user research as a full substitute for market research.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A lead-user project runs in stages (rough 5-6 weeks each): planning -> identify trends/needs -> preliminary concept generation -> final concept generation. Limitations: identifying lead users is hard and needs an expansive, convincing search; lead users (and analogous-market users) are NOT necessarily the common user or early adopters, so their specs suit themselves, not the mass market; therefore lead-user research must be COMPLEMENTED by traditional large-sample market research. Scissors examples (multi-blade for uniform cuts; laser-pointer for straight lines) show lead-user insights that also help common users.

distractors.wrong: Lead users are easy to identify and recruit
distractors.why: identifying them needs an expansive, convincing search; it is one of the main limitations

distractors.wrong: Lead-user specifications directly suit the mass market
distractors.why: their specs suit themselves; insights must be adapted and validated with common-user market research

nodes.sample_question: What are the main limitations of using lead users, and how are they mitigated? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Overgeneralising lead-user preferences to the mass market.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Peter Morville's UX honeycomb evaluates whether a product delivers a superior experience around a central 'VALUABLE' cell via six facets: USEFUL (does it meet a need?), USABLE (easy to use?), DESIRABLE (image/identity/brand value?), FINDABLE (easy to search/identify features?), ACCESSIBLE (usable by people with disabilities?), and CREDIBLE (do users trust the offering/communication?). Together these dimensions build a superior user experience.

distractors.wrong: The honeycomb's facets are mainly about visual aesthetics
distractors.why: they cover usefulness, usability, findability, accessibility and credibility — not just looks

distractors.wrong: 'Accessible' means available in many stores
distractors.why: in the honeycomb 'accessible' means usable by people with disabilities, not distribution reach

nodes.sample_question: Name the facets of Peter Morville's user-experience honeycomb and what each checks. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing UX to usability/aesthetics and omitting findable/accessible/credible.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Sources of user information rank by reach vs experience required: lead-user research (rich experience), QFD (moderate experience, more users), idea competitions, and crowdsourcing (most users, varied experience). New-product research DIFFERS from existing-product research: it does not need large samples or routine customer-service data; instead carefully choose a few users and non-users to identify MISSING needs and gaps. Research shows ~30 interviews identify 90-95% of needs (interviews reach saturation). Questions cover typical uses, likes, dislikes and suggestions; focus groups reveal insights individual interviews miss.

distractors.wrong: New-product market research needs very large samples like existing-product research
distractors.why: ~30 well-chosen users identify 90-95% of needs; the goal is missing-need discovery, not large-sample measurement

distractors.wrong: Focus groups and individual interviews yield identical insight
distractors.why: focus-group interaction reveals insights that individual interviews do not

nodes.sample_question: How does market research for a NEW product differ from research on an existing product, and why are ~30 interviews often enough? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Applying large-sample existing-product survey logic to new-product gap discovery.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Kano classifies user-need attributes into five types: (1) MUST-HAVE (basic; absence -> rejection, presence adds no extra satisfaction); (2) ATTRACTIVE/delighter (unexpected; absence not missed, presence boosts satisfaction and can command a premium); (3) ONE-DIMENSIONAL/performance (satisfaction rises linearly with amount; customers pay more for more, e.g. storage capacity — offer configurations); (4) INDIFFERENT (no impact — exclude); (5) REVERSE (negative — its presence causes rejection — exclude). Use Kano to prioritise: meet must-haves, add one-dimensional configurations, infuse attractive features for premium, and avoid indifferent/reverse attributes.

distractors.wrong: Adding more of a must-have keeps increasing satisfaction
distractors.why: must-haves only prevent dissatisfaction; beyond the minimum they add no extra satisfaction (that is one-dimensional)

distractors.wrong: Attractive and one-dimensional attributes are the same
distractors.why: attractive = unexpected delighters (premium); one-dimensional = expected, satisfaction scales linearly with quantity

nodes.sample_question: Name the five Kano attribute categories and explain how a must-have differs from an attractive attribute. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing must-have (saturating) with one-dimensional (linear) and attractive (delighter) attributes.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Built on Kano, the Product Variety Matrix crosses SATISFIER levels (one-dimensional: minimum, satisfier-1, satisfier-2) against DELIGHTER levels (attractive: no-delighter, delighter-1, delighter-2), giving 3x3 = NINE configurations of a single product. The minimum-satisfier/no-delighter cell is the must-have base; higher cells add premium. Variety lets different customers pick a configuration within their budget (e.g. three laptop configs at a 50,000 budget), giving competitive advantage. More variety attracts customers seeking a specific configuration.

distractors.wrong: The Product Variety Matrix produces three product versions
distractors.why: two satisfier levels x two delighter levels around the base give NINE configurations

distractors.wrong: Variety means one premium model only
distractors.why: the point is multiple configurations so customers self-select within budget; one model defeats the purpose

nodes.sample_question: Explain how the Product Variety Matrix generates nine configurations and the benefit of offering them. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Miscounting the grid (it is 3x3 = 9) or missing the budget-self-selection benefit.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The House of Quality is the core QFD diagram that collates all product information in one picture. LEFT side: customer needs/benefits (voice of customer, from market research, with importance ratings). TOP: technical responses/specifications needed to meet those needs. MIDDLE (body): the RELATIONSHIP matrix linking customer needs to technical specs (strong/moderate/weak). ROOF (triangle): technical CORRELATIONS between specs (positive/negative). RIGHT: PLANNING matrix benchmarking your product vs competitors on customer needs. BOTTOM: technical competitive assessment / targets. One diagram gives designers customer + technical + competitor information together.

distractors.wrong: The roof of the House of Quality shows customer-vs-competitor comparison
distractors.why: the roof shows technical-spec CORRELATIONS; the customer-vs-competitor comparison is the right-hand planning matrix

distractors.wrong: The House of Quality only lists customer requirements
distractors.why: it also holds technical specs, the relationship matrix, technical correlations, and competitor benchmarks

nodes.sample_question: Label the parts of the House of Quality (left, top, middle, roof, right, bottom) and state what each contains. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Mixing up the roof (technical correlations) with the right-side planning matrix (competitor benchmark).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: QFD is a documented process (invented in the mid-20th-century Japanese auto industry) that DEPLOYS customer needs into technical specifications, ensuring consumer needs stay the focus of the NPD process. It cascades through levels: system -> subsystem/part -> component -> process control. By front-loading clarity it pushes design changes EARLIER (cheaper) and reduces costly late changes. Benefits: increased customer satisfaction, enhanced quality, lower cost (fewer late changes), on-schedule delivery, better cross-functional knowledge transfer and a common visual language. QFD is complex — appropriate for complex products, overkill for simple ones.

distractors.wrong: QFD increases late-stage design changes
distractors.why: QFD front-loads clarity so design changes happen EARLY (cheap) and late changes fall, possibly to zero

distractors.wrong: QFD is worthwhile for every product
distractors.why: it is complex and best for complex products; for simple products it is overkill

nodes.sample_question: What does QFD deploy, and list four benefits of using it. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Claiming QFD raises late changes (it lowers them) or applying it to trivially simple products.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.formula: technical_weight = SUM_over_needs( customer_importance x relationship_score[9/3/1] ); relative_% = technical_weight / grand_total

variables.relationship_score: strength of need-to-spec link: 9 strong, 3 moderate, 1 weak
variables.grand_total: sum of all technical column weights

nodes.teaching_note: To prioritise technical requirements in the House of Quality, weight each technical spec by the customer importance of every need it serves times the relationship strength, then sum down the column. Relationship strengths are typically coded 9 (strong), 3 (moderate), 1 (weak). For each technical column: weight = sum over needs of (customer_importance x relationship_score). Convert to a relative % = column_weight / total_of_all_columns. Pressure-cooker example: cooking-pressure weight = (5x9)+(4x9)+(5x9)+(5x3)+(4x1)+(... ) ... totalling 190; with grand total 999, cooking-pressure relative weight = 190/999 ~= 19%. The highest-% specs are the design priorities. ALWAYS recompute and verify the arithmetic before presenting.

distractors.wrong: Relationship strength is added, not multiplied by customer importance
distractors.why: each cell = customer_importance x relationship_score (9/3/1); these products are summed down the column

distractors.wrong: Relative weight is the raw column total
distractors.why: relative weight = column_total / grand_total of all columns (e.g. 190/999 ~= 19%)

nodes.sample_question: In a House of Quality, customer needs rated 5,4,5 for safety/fast-cooking/ease relate to 'cooking pressure' at 9,9,3. Compute the column weight for cooking pressure. (1M)
nodes.failure_mode: Adding instead of multiplying importance x relationship, or forgetting to normalise by the grand total.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: User toolkits let users design/customise products themselves, shifting experimentation to the user. They are an effective response to HETEROGENEOUS demand that is hard for the firm to meet directly, and they gather user information. The user creates the prototype; the firm produces it. Examples: airline itinerary search, insurance/mutual-fund product selection, IC-design simulators, fashion accessory patterns, jewellery video try-on, fast-food order codes, configurable Dell laptops, paint-shade mixing. Toolkits enable users to customise to taste and discover new configurations the firm could not pre-specify.

distractors.wrong: Toolkits mean the firm designs every variant in advance
distractors.why: the USER designs/experiments; the firm only produces the chosen configuration

distractors.wrong: Toolkits suit homogeneous demand best
distractors.why: they are a response to HETEROGENEOUS demand that is hard for the firm to meet directly

nodes.sample_question: What problem do user toolkits solve, and how do they shift the design role? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking the firm still pre-designs variants instead of the user experimenting.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: An effective toolkit must: enable complete TRIAL-AND-ERROR learning cycles by the user; offer an adequate SOLUTION SPACE covering high-potential designs; be USER-FRIENDLY (users apply their own design language/skills); contain a LIBRARY of commonly used modules; and translate the user's design into a producible product without major revisions (no dissonance). Value: competitive advantage that is hard to copy (first-mover learning), and it cuts development time because trial-and-error cycles are done by the user, not the developer. Firms also learn user trends.

distractors.wrong: A toolkit only needs to look user-friendly
distractors.why: it must also support full trial-error cycles, an adequate solution space, a module library and revision-free translation to production

distractors.wrong: Toolkits increase the firm's development time
distractors.why: they CUT development time by moving trial-and-error cycles to the user

nodes.sample_question: List the requirements for an effective user toolkit and the competitive advantage it confers. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Listing only usability and missing the solution-space, module-library and clean-translation requirements.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Evaluating innovations uses several methods: scoring/screening of product concepts; concept testing with trials and market research; the risk-payoff matrix at each stage; evaluating early prototypes with real users to find flaws; and treating each stage as a real OPTION — weighing the cost-benefit of delaying decisions under uncertainty. Every feature involves a cost-benefit; assess at each stage before committing. The ATAR model then estimates demand.

distractors.wrong: Innovation is evaluated once, at launch
distractors.why: evaluation is staged: scoring, concept testing, risk-payoff and real-options checks happen throughout the funnel

distractors.wrong: Every feature should be added if customers like it
distractors.why: each feature carries a cost-benefit that must be assessed; not all clear the bar

nodes.sample_question: List the methods used to evaluate innovations during the NPD funnel. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating evaluation as a one-shot gate rather than a staged, cost-benefit process.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The risk-payoff matrix crosses the DECISION (stop vs continue the project) with the OUTCOME (would fail vs would succeed). Two cells are correct (stop a would-fail; continue a would-succeed) and two are errors: continuing a project that fails (a 'go' error / commission) and stopping a project that would have succeeded (a 'drop' error / omission — e.g. a competitor later succeeds with it). Managers can't always be right, so understand the probability of success and manage risk via four strategies: AVOID (drop the risky project, incurring opportunity cost), MITIGATE (reduce execution risk — backup options, extra channels, redesign), TRANSFER (shift risk via JV/subcontractor/franchise, e.g. McDonald's franchising), and ACCEPT (contingency plan = active acceptance; or passive acceptance).

distractors.wrong: Stopping a project is always the safe, error-free choice
distractors.why: stopping a would-succeed project is a 'drop' error of omission — an error just as real as continuing a failure

distractors.wrong: Transferring risk means eliminating it
distractors.why: transfer shifts responsibility to another party (JV/subcontractor/franchise); the risk still exists, just borne elsewhere

nodes.sample_question: Name the two error types in the risk-payoff matrix and the four risk-handling strategies. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Recognising only the 'continue-and-fail' error while missing the 'stop-a-winner' (omission) error.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Concept testing is a prescreening step BEFORE the development/execution stage with two aims: eliminate poor concepts and produce a rough high-level estimate. It surveys potential customers on intention to use, typically a five-point purchase-intent scale (definitely buy / probably buy / might buy / probably not / definitely not), tracking the top two boxes. Formats escalate in cost: verbal description -> description with sketch/picture -> physical prototype/sample. A key debate is whether to include a PRICE tag: include it to capture the full purchase decision, or omit it to get unbiased reaction to the product itself. Define the respondent group and the mode of reaching them.

distractors.wrong: Concept testing gives a precise demand forecast
distractors.why: it gives a ROUGH high-level estimate and screens out poor concepts, not a precise forecast

distractors.wrong: You must always state the price in a concept test
distractors.why: it is a deliberate choice: include price for the full decision, or omit it for unbiased product reaction

nodes.sample_question: What are the two objectives of concept testing, and what is the price-tag trade-off? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Expecting precision from concept testing and forgetting the price-inclusion trade-off.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Conjoint/joint-space analysis interprets concept-test responses to locate a product in BENEFIT space and identify which segment it serves. By scoring a product on attributes (e.g. fashion vs comfort, or experience/performance/safety/price seekers in autos) and running cluster analysis / factor scores / regressions, the firm maps its product and competitors on a perceptual (joint-space) map. This reveals the segment actually targeted versus what designers intended, who the direct competition is, and how to set price relative to competitors' positions (e.g. FASTag toll-discount decisions).

distractors.wrong: Conjoint analysis tells you only whether customers like the product
distractors.why: it locates the product among benefit SEGMENTS and competitors on a perceptual map — segment positioning, not just liking

distractors.wrong: Designers' intended positioning always matches how customers perceive it
distractors.why: conjoint often reveals customers cluster the product differently from the designer's intent

nodes.sample_question: How does conjoint/joint-space analysis help interpret concept-test responses? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reading conjoint as a like/dislike score rather than a segment-and-competitor positioning tool.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.formula: Demand = Market_Size x Awareness x Trial x Availability x Repeat (all as fractions)
nodes.teaching_note: ATAR forecasts demand for a new product as the PRODUCT of four fractions: AWARENESS (share who become aware, via advertising) x TRIAL (share of aware who try/buy on trial) x AVAILABILITY (distribution reach in the target market) x REPEAT (share who repeat-purchase, or for big-ticket items recommend). Demand (units/adopters) = market_size x A x T x Av x R. Because it is multiplicative, a weak link (e.g. poor availability) collapses demand even with high awareness. Forecasts are rough; crosscheck assumptions and revise A,T,Av,R against real results next period. ATAR is also a launch checklist: ensure enough advertising (awareness), trial packs/test drives (trial), distribution (availability) and repeat/word-of-mouth.

distractors.wrong: ATAR demand is the sum of awareness, trial, availability and repeat
distractors.why: the four are MULTIPLIED, not added; a low factor (e.g. availability) collapses total demand

distractors.wrong: Repeat purchase is irrelevant for big-ticket items
distractors.why: for big-ticket items 'repeat' is captured as recommendation/word-of-mouth to others considering the product

nodes.sample_question: A new snack reaches 50% awareness, 40% trial among aware, 60% availability and 50% repeat in a 2,000,000 market. Estimate adopters using ATAR. (1M)
nodes.failure_mode: Adding the ATAR factors instead of multiplying them, or ignoring availability/repeat.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Evaluate a concept on multiple dimensions: STRATEGIC FIT (with corporate vision/objectives); CUSTOMER FIT (meets a real consumer need, good perceived value, increases loyalty); MARKET ATTRACTIVENESS (unique, can reach #1/#2 and meaningful share); TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY (buildable and protectable/hard to copy -> competitive advantage); and FINANCIAL RETURNS (likely break-even, acceptable timeline, required earnings in time). The Jio example: technically feasible, strategically relevant ('new oil is data'), strong customer fit (free service built awareness fast), creating market dominance and faster break-even via a large subscriber base.

distractors.wrong: A concept only needs good financial returns to pass
distractors.why: it must also fit strategy, the customer, market attractiveness and be technically feasible/protectable

distractors.wrong: Strategic fit and customer fit are the same dimension
distractors.why: strategic fit = alignment with corporate vision; customer fit = meeting consumer need/value — distinct checks

nodes.sample_question: List the dimensions on which a new product concept should be evaluated. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Collapsing evaluation to financials and ignoring strategic/customer/feasibility fit.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The product protocol is the final definition/agreement that emerges from the concept stage — the 'definition of the product'. It articulates the target market, positioning, and the product's attributes, benefits, functions and features/usage. It is the package outcome (product requirements/deliverables) that hands clarity to the design/development stage. Example: a soft drink targeting youth, positioned as a healthier drink, with attributes = health benefits over traditional drinks plus its functions/features of use.

distractors.wrong: The product protocol is the early rough idea
distractors.why: it is the FINAL agreed definition (target, positioning, attributes/benefits/features) handed to development

distractors.wrong: The protocol is the same as the mission statement
distractors.why: the mission statement opens the process; the protocol is the concept-stage output that defines the product for development

nodes.sample_question: What is the product protocol and what does it articulate? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the final protocol with the opening mission statement/charter.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Project selection combines FINANCIAL analysis (ROI, payback period, IRR — used as guidance, since projections are imprecise) with MANAGERIAL analysis (strategic fit, internal capability, resource/portfolio constraints). Because resources (capital, people) are finite, prioritise by fitment. Strategic approaches: TOP-DOWN (HQ/SBU sets strategy and allocates funds) or BOTTOM-UP (project teams apply mission/competency criteria to filter); better firms blend both. A 7-point scoring model covers management interest, customer interest, sustainability of competitive advantage, technical feasibility, business-case strength, fit with core competencies, and profitability impact.

distractors.wrong: Financial projections alone should decide project selection
distractors.why: projections are imprecise guidance; managerial fit, capability and resource constraints matter as much

distractors.wrong: Top-down and bottom-up selection are mutually exclusive
distractors.why: better-performing firms blend both top-down funding and bottom-up team filtering

nodes.sample_question: How do financial and managerial analyses combine in new-product project selection? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Over-trusting imprecise financial projections and ignoring strategic-fit/capability screens.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Rubbermaid (later acquired by Newell) makes hundreds of thousands of non-fancy household plastic/rubber items, with ~90% new-product success and ~30% of sales from products under five years old. Innovation is MARKET-driven (not technology-driven): incremental design tweaks from understanding customer problems (e.g. plastic bucket -> add lid -> foot lever -> wheels for commercial use; thin dustpan edge from watching a hotel doorman). Ideas come from focus groups, encouraging staff to read complaints, and solving customer problems at all levels. Newell kept Rubbermaid's plants/culture separate to preserve its innovation capability.

distractors.wrong: Rubbermaid's edge was high technology
distractors.why: its innovation is MARKET-driven incremental design from customer problems, not high tech

distractors.wrong: Acquirers should fully integrate an innovative target
distractors.why: Newell kept Rubbermaid separate to preserve its distinct product-innovation culture

nodes.sample_question: What kind of innovation drives Rubbermaid, and how does it generate ideas? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming product-innovation success requires technology rather than market-driven incremental design.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Chipotle (Steve Ells, Denver 1993) began as a quick burrito shop to fund a planned fine-dining restaurant, but the model that accidentally worked was 'fast-casual': a simple, limited, made-to-order menu with skilled fresh preparation served quickly — between fast food and full-service. Success factors: simple menu (no heavy pre-preparation), made-to-order customisation, open kitchen signalling freshness, and a 'food with integrity' vision EXECUTED (not advertised) — growth came by word of mouth. Lesson: execution and fit-with-customers can matter more than the original plan; let the product do the talking.

distractors.wrong: Chipotle's success came from a planned fast-casual strategy
distractors.why: fast-casual was discovered by accident while funding a fine-dining dream; execution/fit drove it

distractors.wrong: 'Food with integrity' worked because of heavy advertising
distractors.why: it was barely advertised; integrity was EXECUTED (fresh, open kitchen) and spread by word of mouth

nodes.sample_question: What is the 'fast-casual' positioning and what made Chipotle work? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Crediting a deliberate strategy/advertising rather than emergent fit and execution.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Good vs bad design is judged more by intuition, experience and understanding of the customer than by formula (e.g. a vacuum too heavy for an elderly user is bad design; an Apple laptop's font/keyboard layout is good). Design synthesises technology with human needs into manufacturable products (ergonomics + art/sensibility). MARKET-driven design responds to expressed customer wants; DESIGN-DRIVEN innovation pushes new MEANINGS/experiences customers didn't ask for (iTunes/iPod redefined using music) — Steve Jobs argued customers can't always articulate new meanings. Design-driven firms create trends rather than follow them.

distractors.wrong: Design quality can be judged by a precise academic formula
distractors.why: it is largely intuition/experience/customer understanding; 'good design' resists a single formula

distractors.wrong: Design-driven innovation just follows expressed customer wants
distractors.why: design-driven innovation pushes NEW meanings customers didn't ask for (iPod/iTunes); market-driven follows expressed wants

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish market-driven from design-driven innovation, with an example. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating all design with responding to stated wants, missing meaning-driven innovation.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Product architecture is the structure within a product. MODULAR architecture (e.g. desktop PC) uses independent, standardised, interchangeable modules -> easy upgrades/repair/reuse, customisation and greater product variety; it optimises FLEXIBILITY over performance/form. INTEGRAL architecture (e.g. laptop/tablet) packs multiple functions into combined parts -> compactness, higher quality/robustness, better performance and form factor, but limited post-purchase change/repair/upgrade and limited variety. The trade-off: modularity = flexibility & variety; integral = form, performance & quality.

distractors.wrong: Integral architecture gives more flexibility for upgrades
distractors.why: INTEGRAL limits post-purchase upgrades; MODULAR is the flexible, upgradeable one

distractors.wrong: Modular architecture gives the most compact, highest-performance product
distractors.why: compactness/performance/form come from INTEGRAL; modularity trades those for flexibility/variety

nodes.sample_question: Contrast modular and integral product architecture on flexibility, variety and form/performance. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping the trade-offs (assigning flexibility to integral or compactness to modular).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Six modularity types: (1) COMPONENT-SHARING — same component across many products (e.g. one processor across models); (2) COMPONENT-SWAPPING — different components on a common base via a standard interface (e.g. same socket, swap battery); (3) CUT-TO-FIT — a base material cut/lengthened to size (e.g. trousers/wire covers cut to length); (4) MIX — base materials combined to create new variants (e.g. mixing paint colours); (5) BUS — a common base plate/board onto which multiple components mount (e.g. circuit board with ports); (6) SECTIONAL — sections fit together to build a larger structure (e.g. Lego toys).

distractors.wrong: Component-sharing and component-swapping are the same
distractors.why: sharing uses ONE common component across products; swapping puts DIFFERENT components on a common base via a standard interface

distractors.wrong: Sectional modularity means cutting a base material to length
distractors.why: that is CUT-TO-FIT; sectional joins sections into a larger structure (Lego)

nodes.sample_question: Name the six types of modularity and give an example of each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing sharing vs swapping, or cut-to-fit vs sectional.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: DFM designs a product for easy, low-cost manufacturing using techniques: MINIMISE the number of parts; use COMMON parts across products; ELIMINATE fasteners (cut assembly time); eliminate JIGS/FIXTURES and ADJUSTMENTS during assembly; and ELIMINATE ERRORS by design (e.g. colour coding, asymmetric/poka-yoke shapes). Further: hand final assembly to the customer (IKEA) to cut transport/cost; minimise system complexity; isolate frequently-replaced parts (modular) for easy replacement. Lower manufacturing cost opens a larger market.

distractors.wrong: DFM mainly means adding more precise fasteners and adjustments
distractors.why: DFM ELIMINATES fasteners, jigs and adjustments and minimises parts to cut cost/time

distractors.wrong: DFM is unrelated to market size
distractors.why: lower manufacturing cost from DFM lowers price and opens a larger market

nodes.sample_question: List five Design-for-Manufacturing techniques and how they reduce cost. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Listing techniques that add complexity instead of removing parts/fasteners/adjustments.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Two cases show architecture choices flipping an industry. SWATCH responded to cheap Japanese quartz watches by adopting INTEGRAL architecture (first in watches): drastic parts reduction, components on a sealed base plate, automated assembly, rugged materials -> low cost + high reliability, while keeping high VARIETY on the outside via 200-300 modular dial designs. SHIMANO turned a fragmented modular bicycle-component market into a consolidated one by INTEGRATING components into an optimised 'click-shift' gear KIT; users accepted the optimised set over mixing parts, branding became visible, and by 1997 Shimano held ~86-98% gear market share. Lesson: integral/modular choice is strategic and can dominate an industry.

distractors.wrong: Swatch succeeded by making watches fully modular and repairable
distractors.why: Swatch went INTEGRAL (sealed, drastically fewer parts) for low cost/reliability, with modular DIALS only for variety

distractors.wrong: Shimano won by selling loose, mix-and-match components
distractors.why: Shimano won by INTEGRATING components into one optimised gear kit, consolidating a fragmented market

nodes.sample_question: How did Swatch and Shimano use integral vs modular architecture to dominate their industries? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reversing each firm's architecture choice or missing that the choice was strategic.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.concept: Design for the new product process
nodes.teaching_note: Beyond manufacturability, design choices serve other goals: SPEED to market (e.g. lighter ergonomic Ingersoll grinder shapes); DIFFERENTIATION / user-centric design (SUVs blending car comfort with clearance; JCB heavy-equipment design language); UNIVERSAL design (automatic mall doors usable by all ages, frequent use); CORPORATE IDENTITY (consistent look/feel — TATA/Maruti grilles, Apple, Rolex); and DESIGN FOR ENVIRONMENT (recycled/reusable/green materials). Design is a deliberate lever across the whole NPD process, not just aesthetics.

distractors.wrong: Design only affects how a product looks
distractors.why: design also drives speed-to-market, differentiation, universal usability, corporate identity and environmental impact

distractors.wrong: Corporate-identity design is the same as universal design
distractors.why: corporate identity = consistent brand look/feel; universal design = usable across all ages/abilities

nodes.sample_question: Give four product-process goals (besides manufacturability) that design choices can serve. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing design to aesthetics and missing speed/identity/universal/environment roles.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Prototypes are product APPROXIMATIONS used for testing, learning, communication and integration of components; they reduce time, cost and risk (errors caught late are costly) and act as funding MILESTONES/interim-success demonstrations. ANALYTICAL prototypes (computer/3D-CAD models, simulations) allow flexible non-destructive testing; PHYSICAL prototypes detect unanticipated real-world issues simulation misses. Prototypes show feasibility for breakthrough products, aid problem detection for derivatives, and plan releases for platform products. In complex projects use MULTIPLE, well-spaced prototype cycles so learning from one feeds the next; target users evaluate prototypes to surface flaws.

distractors.wrong: Prototypes are only built once the product is nearly final
distractors.why: prototypes are used throughout as approximations/milestones to learn and de-risk early, not just at the end

distractors.wrong: Computer/analytical prototypes can replace physical prototypes entirely
distractors.why: physical prototypes catch unanticipated real-world issues that simulations miss; both are needed

nodes.sample_question: What functions do prototypes serve, and how do analytical and physical prototypes differ? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating prototypes as a final-stage formality or assuming simulation replaces physical testing.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Prototyping strategy seeks fit between the development process and the prototyping method; a key choice is build IN-HOUSE vs via a VENDOR. In-house pros: greater SECRECY (protect competitive advantage before launch) and highly-skilled control — but skilled prototype workers may not transfer well to mass production. Vendor pros: earlier detection of PRODUCTION problems, an objective outside view, easier scale-up and faster transfer to manufacturing (the vendor already knows production mode) — but less secrecy. Choose by weighing secrecy vs production-readiness.

distractors.wrong: Outsourcing prototyping to a vendor maximises secrecy
distractors.why: IN-HOUSE maximises secrecy; vendors see the design, but they catch production problems earlier

distractors.wrong: In-house prototyping always transfers smoothly to mass production
distractors.why: highly-skilled in-house prototypers may not transfer to less-skilled mass production; vendors ease that transition

nodes.sample_question: Compare in-house vs vendor prototyping on secrecy and production-readiness. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming vendors are more secret or that in-house always scales to production.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Gillette kept #1 in razors for decades by continuously innovating the BLADE. The Mach3 (3-blade) required solving design problems unproven in a twin-blade system: an internal prototype code-named 'Manx' tested blade POSITIONING (each blade closer to the face and to each other to cut closely while reducing irritation), pivot/pressure points, handle placement, and a fading lubricating-strip indicator. Concept-to-launch took ~6 years (3 years development, 1995-98) and ~$750M (4x the prior launch); consumers were price-insensitive, willing to pay a ~35-45% premium. Gillette later bypassed 4-blade rivals straight to the 5-blade Fusion. Lesson: disciplined prototyping/user-testing cycles de-risk a breakthrough.

distractors.wrong: Gillette rushed Mach3 to market to beat rivals
distractors.why: it spent ~6 years and ~$750M on prototyping/testing before launch; discipline, not speed, drove it

distractors.wrong: Customers refused to pay more for the new razor
distractors.why: user tests showed customers were price-insensitive, paying a ~35-45% premium over the prior product

nodes.sample_question: What did the 'Manx' prototype test, and what does Mach3 illustrate about prototyping breakthroughs? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Missing the multi-year, high-cost disciplined prototyping behind the breakthrough.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: NPD is a cross-functional system; setting up the team is essential because design/modularity choices create conflicts across functions. Which department LEADS depends on where the greatest DEGREE OF CHANGE sits (e.g. material/R&D leads a blade innovation). Complex, long-run projects need strong integration, coordination, communication and collaboration across large multi-skilled teams. Consider co-locating specialists, moving/cross-training people, joint cross-department decisions, informal idea-exchange spaces, and tailored incentive systems (R&D vs shop-floor differ); HR helps set compensation so different teams are incentivised to work together.

distractors.wrong: The marketing department always leads NPD
distractors.why: leadership depends on where the greatest degree of change is (e.g. R&D/materials for a technology-led product)

distractors.wrong: One incentive system fits all NPD team members
distractors.why: R&D and shop-floor work/conditions differ; incentives must be tailored, with HR's help

nodes.sample_question: What determines which function leads an NPD project, and what does cross-functional integration require? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming a fixed lead function and uniform incentives across the team.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Three structures: FUNCTIONAL — the product moves department to department until done; good for functional specialisation and customised projects, but poor coordination, slow, no single owner, end-to-end visibility limited. PROJECT — a dedicated team works 100% on one new product to launch; shortens time, better coordination, suits breakthroughs/startups, but expertise is tied up and unavailable to other projects, and functional specialisation is limited. MATRIX — DUAL reporting (functional manager for technical depth + project manager for the new-product activity); suits complex, long-gestation projects (autos 2-3 yrs, aerospace a decade). Matrix has two versions: HEAVYWEIGHT (project manager has high discretionary power over functional heads) and LIGHTWEIGHT (project manager mainly coordinates, less power).

distractors.wrong: A matrix structure means a single reporting line
distractors.why: matrix means DUAL reporting to both a functional and a project manager

distractors.wrong: Functional structure is best for breakthrough startups
distractors.why: PROJECT structure suits breakthroughs/startups; functional suits customised, specialisation-heavy work

nodes.sample_question: Describe functional, project and matrix NPD structures and the heavyweight/lightweight matrix variants. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the structures or forgetting matrix's dual-reporting and heavyweight/lightweight split.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Match the organisation structure to the project type: RADICAL/breakthrough -> PROJECT (dedicated) structure; deep TECHNICAL-EXPERTISE / specialised-skill projects -> FUNCTIONAL structure; SYSTEM-solution / new-PLATFORM projects -> HEAVYWEIGHT matrix (powerful project manager); DERIVATIVE/ENHANCEMENT projects -> LIGHTWEIGHT matrix (coordinating project manager). Firms tend to have a dominant structure tied to their product type and find it hard to switch (rigidities); the leading function often varies (R&D leads drug development; design leads furniture).

distractors.wrong: A derivative enhancement project needs a heavyweight project structure
distractors.why: derivative/enhancement suits a LIGHTWEIGHT matrix; heavyweight matrix fits new-platform/system solutions

distractors.wrong: Firms switch NPD structures easily as needed
distractors.why: firms have a dominant structure and face rigidities switching (e.g. functional to project)

nodes.sample_question: Match project types (breakthrough, deep-tech, platform, derivative) to the appropriate organisation structure. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Mismatching project type to structure (e.g. heavyweight matrix for a small derivative).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Product integrity is the high CONSISTENCY of a differentiated product that creates instant appeal and a 'wow'/X-factor — a harmony of the product/service with the user's lifestyle and a balance among product features; it is subtle and reflects the organisation. Two parts: INTERNAL integrity = consistency/fit between the organisation's functions and structure and how the product's parts/layouts work together; EXTERNAL integrity = fit between product performance and user expectations, objectives, values and lifestyle. Effective LEADERSHIP drives integrity: leaders/heavyweight project managers keep teams focused on user expectations and infuse the 'soul' of the product (Apple, Gillette obsession with blade quality).

distractors.wrong: Product integrity is just product functionality working
distractors.why: integrity is broader: harmony with the user's lifestyle and consistency across functions, creating the wow factor

distractors.wrong: Internal and external integrity are the same
distractors.why: internal = function/structure/parts fit inside; external = product performance vs user expectations/values

nodes.sample_question: Define product integrity and distinguish its internal and external forms. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing integrity to 'it works' and conflating internal vs external integrity.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Pure services are hard to develop/sell because of INTANGIBILITY — clients can't see/test the result and are sceptical about the outcome, and quality is hard to specify/measure. PRODUCTIZING a service makes it tangible and easier to purchase, budget and trust, and lowers the risk of cost overruns/poor results. To productize: give the service a descriptive NAME, define a TIME FRAME, attach a PRICE tag, define the model/process; offer customised service PACKAGES for user groups (e.g. annual maintenance contracts); and create interlinked service modules purchasable with or without prior commitment (e.g. car bundled with free servicing). Banking example: turn 'account opening' into a standardised product module.

distractors.wrong: Services are easy to sell because they have no inventory
distractors.why: intangibility makes services HARD to sell/evaluate; productizing them is the remedy

distractors.wrong: Productizing a service means making a physical product
distractors.why: it means giving the service a name, time frame, price and defined process so it feels product-like and tangible

nodes.sample_question: Why are pure services hard to sell, and how does productizing them help? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring intangibility and the productization remedy (name/time/price/process).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A PSS is a marketable combination of products and services along the spectrum between pure product and pure service; bundling differentiating services reduces commoditisation and lifts profit, and creates value four ways: cost reduction, better asset utilisation, expanded customer base, and resistance to competition. Three types: (1) PRODUCT-ORIENTED — user OWNS the product; firm maintains it (AMCs, consumables, advice, buy-back) e.g. water purifier/washing machine; (2) USE-ORIENTED — FIRM owns; user rents/shares/leases the function for a period e.g. tent/bicycle/tool sharing, libraries; (3) RESULT-ORIENTED — user pays for the RESULT/outcome; the product is replaced by a service e.g. voicemail vs answering machine, Netflix/movie rental, pay-per-output.

distractors.wrong: In a use-oriented PSS the customer owns the product
distractors.why: in USE-oriented PSS the FIRM owns it and the user rents/shares; the user owns it only in PRODUCT-oriented PSS

distractors.wrong: Result-oriented PSS means selling the physical product
distractors.why: result-oriented replaces the product with a service — the user pays for the outcome (e.g. voicemail, Netflix)

nodes.sample_question: Name the three types of Product Service System and who owns the product in each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing who owns the product across product-/use-/result-oriented PSS.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Platform thinking builds a common service ARCHITECTURE (shared subsystems and interfaces) that supports high service variety and can be extended into new business models, holding the organisation's capabilities/insights in reusable modules. A core banking platform (e.g. Infosys Finacle, refined with ICICI as lead user) becomes a base of modules (account opening, treasury, lending, repayment) extended to new bank clients with limited customisation. SuperSeva (Bangalore concierge, 87 services) shows the logic: robust modular processes, SLA tracking, cost reduction per service, free high-frequency services to drive float, hard-to-match scale + scope -> near-monopoly.

distractors.wrong: Platform thinking means building each service from scratch
distractors.why: it builds REUSABLE modules on a common architecture, extended across clients with limited customisation

distractors.wrong: SuperSeva competes mainly on price for single services
distractors.why: its advantage is scale + scope (87 services, robust modular processes, free high-frequency services) that rivals can't match

nodes.sample_question: What is platform thinking for services, and how did SuperSeva use it to build an advantage? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating platform services as bespoke builds rather than reusable modular architecture.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: New-product teams need an expert product manager and a CULTURE of collaboration and creativity, because NPD integrates marketing, R&D, manufacturing, sales and design. Collaboration must produce SYNERGY (output greater than the sum of parts — '2+2>4') with clear ownership, no hidden agendas, and everyone aligned to the goal. The Pixar case shows culture as a hard-to-copy advantage: Pixar merged creative storytelling with pioneering 3D computer-graphics technology by physically intermingling content creators and technologists, with Steve Jobs as sponsor bringing key people together; Disney acquired Pixar (2005-06) yet let it run independently to preserve the culture (as Newell did with Rubbermaid).

distractors.wrong: Synergy means each member simply doing their own job well
distractors.why: synergy is collective output greater than the sum of parts (2+2>4), from collaboration, not isolated effort

distractors.wrong: Acquirers should absorb a creative team into their bureaucracy
distractors.why: Disney/Newell kept Pixar/Rubbermaid independent to protect the hard-to-copy creative culture

nodes.sample_question: Why is culture central to NPD teams, and what does the Pixar case illustrate about synergy? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Missing synergy and the need to protect a distinct innovation culture post-acquisition.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: NPD needs buy-in and OWNERSHIP from everyone (it is created by a set of skilled specialists, not one leader); some teams have a product CHAMPION. Ownership comes from training, EMPOWERMENT and motivation: management gives autonomy and supports/facilitates team decisions rather than ordering, so members feel ownership. Leadership style must SHIFT across stages: in the early, chaotic, many-ideas phase the leader is CREATIVE and inspiring; in the implementation/testing phase the leader is a DISCIPLINARIAN — action-oriented, sticking to timelines and budgets.
