Few people excel at both, so sometimes two leaders or one with both characteristics are needed; a good product leader is a broad general manager with self-confidence and empathy.

distractors.wrong: Ownership is imposed top-down by management orders
distractors.why: ownership comes from empowerment/autonomy and facilitation, not ordering

distractors.wrong: The same leadership style works through all NPD stages
distractors.why: early stages need a creative/inspiring leader; later stages need a disciplined, timeline-driven one

nodes.sample_question: How is ownership built in NPD teams, and how must leadership style change across stages? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming ownership is commanded and one leadership style fits all phases.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Team membership is layered: a CORE team (stays the whole project for continuity — e.g. marketing/R&D leads across a 2-3 year Gillette project); AD HOC teams (join for a specific phase from functional groups, e.g. factory workers in development, sales team at launch, then return to their function); and an EXTENDED team (ecosystem stakeholders — suppliers, dealers, resellers, external research). Roles include product manager/champion (senior, experienced executor), sponsor (executive overseeing accountability/budget — e.g. Steve Jobs at Pixar), strategist/inventor/rationalist, and facilitator. For minor extensions firms may not dedicate a team but use a NETWORK with point-of-contact 'nodes' (e.g. PMO) connecting functions.

distractors.wrong: The whole team stays for the entire project
distractors.why: only the CORE team stays throughout; ad hoc members join per phase and extended members are ecosystem stakeholders

distractors.wrong: Every new product needs a dedicated full team
distractors.why: for minor extensions firms use a network of point-of-contact nodes rather than a dedicated team

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish core, ad hoc and extended teams in NPD. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating membership as one fixed team rather than layered core/ad hoc/extended.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.concept: Managing the NPD team (training & virtual teams)
nodes.teaching_note: Managing NPD teams needs specific, situational skill and a learning orientation. A key requirement is CROSS-FUNCTIONAL training so every member thinks about the impact on the END product (profitability, sellability, manufacturability) rather than only their silo (a technical person beyond technical superiority). Modern NPD teams are increasingly GLOBALLY DISPERSED / VIRTUAL (GDT) across geographies and time zones; this enables 24-hour work, faster scaling and access to region-specific skills, but creates challenges in performance measurement, control, communication (written vs verbal), and cultural differences — requiring strong communication, cohesion and mutual support via Zoom/Teams/scheduled all-hands.

distractors.wrong: NPD team training should deepen each member's own functional silo
distractors.why: the key is CROSS-functional training so each member sees impact on the whole product, not silo depth

distractors.wrong: Global dispersed teams have only advantages
distractors.why: GDTs enable 24-hr work and skill access but add control, measurement, communication and cultural challenges

nodes.sample_question: Why is cross-functional training important for NPD teams, and what challenges do globally dispersed teams add? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Promoting silo training and ignoring the control/communication challenges of virtual teams.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Product use (field/user) testing puts a prototype — an early-to-near-finished product — under NORMAL operating conditions to check that output satisfies requirements and meets customer needs. It is necessary because customer needs are complex and diverse and SIMULATION (computer testing) cannot fully capture real use; it also senses competitive reaction and tests delivery quality. Use the iterative prototype feedback loop (learn -> refine -> repeat until users approve and specs are met). Pre-use testing captures immediate sensory reactions (colour, speed, durability, ergonomics, handling) from real users.

distractors.wrong: Computer simulation can replace product use testing
distractors.why: real, diverse customer needs require field testing under normal operating conditions that simulation can't fully capture

distractors.wrong: Product use testing happens once and is final
distractors.why: it is an iterative feedback loop — learn, refine, retest until users approve and specs are met

nodes.sample_question: Why is product use testing necessary even after simulation, and what does it assess? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Believing simulation substitutes for real-condition use testing.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: ALPHA testing is early, INTERNAL testing with employees/colleagues/staff during development (the product may be only ~30% functional) — a quick check of whether it works and looks right and surfaces surface/technical bugs. BETA testing is short-term external testing at CUSTOMER/CLIENT sites on a near-complete product (~90% functional) before full launch, giving direct user feedback on function/usability (origin: computer hardware/software, e.g. Microsoft Internet Explorer's alpha then public beta releases vs Netscape). Alpha precedes beta. A constraint: TIME PRESSURE near release can compress/skip beta testing, which saves time short-term but causes defects and dissatisfaction long-term, wasting the testing effort.

distractors.wrong: Beta testing is done internally with employees
distractors.why: beta is EXTERNAL at customer/client sites; ALPHA is the internal employee test

distractors.wrong: Alpha tests a ~90% complete product
distractors.why: alpha tests an early ~30%-functional product; ~90% completeness is the beta stage

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish alpha and beta testing by who tests and product completeness. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping alpha (internal/early) and beta (external/near-complete).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Gamma testing tests a FULLY developed, completed product with AMPLE time and no development-time pressure, so end users evaluate the final item in detail with no shortcuts — solving the problem of beta tests that are rushed or use a less-optimised version. It is essential where halfway testing is impossible or dangerous: new MEDICINES (full clinical trials, up to ~10 years), and MEDICAL EQUIPMENT (e.g. CT scanners) tested under many real conditions. The Apple PowerBook example (a fault discovered only after full launch) shows the cost of inadequate final testing. Gamma is costly/time-consuming but necessary in certain industries.

distractors.wrong: Gamma testing is a quick final check like a rushed beta
distractors.why: gamma uses a FULLY developed product with AMPLE time and no time pressure — the opposite of a rushed beta

distractors.wrong: Gamma testing is optional in every industry
distractors.why: in medicines/medical devices full gamma testing is essential and can take years (it can't be done halfway)

nodes.sample_question: What is gamma testing and in which industries is it essential? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating gamma as a quick formality rather than full-product, ample-time testing.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Key product-use-testing decisions: WHO is in the user group (lab personnel/experts/employees vs end users); HOW to reach them (mail/personal contact); WHERE (point of use — home/office/factory — vs a central location/test kitchen); whether to REVEAL the brand or run BLIND testing (revealing creates a halo/bias; blind isolates product feedback, useful for competitive comparison); how much EXPLANATION to give (too much overwhelms, too little leaves customers unclear); and the TEST DESIGN — MONADIC (one product alone), SEQUENTIAL MONADIC (same respondent tests versions back-to-back), PAIRED COMPARISON (your product vs one competitor), STAGGERED PAIRED, TRIANGULAR (your product vs two competitors), or conjoint (multi-product). Crucially, results need BENCHMARK norms — an absolute score (e.g. 65% liking) is meaningless without comparison data (previous winners, competitor scores, agency norms).

distractors.wrong: An absolute liking score (e.g. 65%) is meaningful on its own
distractors.why: scores need benchmark norms; 65% is good vs a 50% past winner but weak vs a 70% one

distractors.wrong: Revealing the brand during testing gives the cleanest feedback
distractors.why: brand reveal creates a halo/bias; BLIND testing isolates true product feedback

nodes.sample_question: List the main decisions in product use testing and explain why benchmark norms matter. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reporting raw scores without benchmarks, or assuming branded testing is unbiased.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Sometimes a good product has no buyers — the gap isn't the product but the market. Firms BUILD markets by finding and fixing the reasons people aren't buying: hidden substitutes/alternatives, cultural mismatches, missing supporting products/services (no dealers, no spares, unclear instructions), and usage difficulty. This needs deep QUALITATIVE research with potential customers, asking: who are the target (and non-target) customers? what are their unmet needs? how do they currently meet the need and does that hurt? does our product solve it? what is the quantifiable benefit, market size, direct competition? can we involve users to co-create, leverage assets for advantage, and generate sustained profits?

distractors.wrong: If a good product doesn't sell, the product must be redesigned
distractors.why: the gap may be the MARKET, not the product; fix reasons-for-not-buying via qualitative research first

distractors.wrong: Building markets relies on large-sample quantitative data
distractors.why: it relies on DEEP QUALITATIVE research with potential customers to uncover reasons for not buying

nodes.sample_question: How does a firm 'build a market' for a good product that isn't selling? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Jumping to redesign instead of diagnosing and fixing reasons for not buying.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Five ways to create more demand for an EXISTING product by enhancing it: (1) UTILITY — add/remove functionality (e.g. touch screen, longer battery); (2) EFFICIENCY — make it operationally better (e.g. built-in antivirus); (3) SAFETY — add safety features (e.g. more airbags); (4) AESTHETICS — improve look/feel/appeal; (5) ERGONOMICS — improve comfort/structure/ease of use. Inputs from product-use testing feed these enhancements.

distractors.wrong: The only way to grow demand is to launch a brand-new product
distractors.why: demand for EXISTING products grows via utility, efficiency, safety, aesthetics and ergonomics enhancements

distractors.wrong: Aesthetics and ergonomics are the same lever
distractors.why: aesthetics = look/feel/appeal; ergonomics = comfort/ease of use — distinct enhancement levers

nodes.sample_question: List the five ways to create demand for an existing product. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming growth requires a new product instead of enhancing the existing one.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Two ways to differentiate and expand demand: HORIZONTAL differentiation appeals to DIFFERENT TASTES within the SAME segment (same quality level) — identify unserved tastes and serve the profitable ones (e.g. saree colours/designs/patterns; same-engine car in many colours). VERTICAL differentiation targets DIFFERENT willingness-to-pay levels (quality tiers) — add features/quality not offered by competitors to appeal to a higher segment, and serve the profitable ones (e.g. silk vs cotton sarees from Rs 200 to Rs 2 lakh; adding luxury/safety to reach a higher price band). Brands make vertical differentiation easier; horizontal differentiation is generally easier than vertical.

distractors.wrong: Vertical differentiation means offering different colours/styles at the same price
distractors.why: that is HORIZONTAL (same segment, different tastes); VERTICAL spans quality/price tiers and willingness to pay

distractors.wrong: Horizontal differentiation targets different income segments
distractors.why: horizontal stays within one segment varying taste; targeting different willingness-to-pay tiers is vertical

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish horizontal and vertical product differentiation, with an example of each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping horizontal (taste, same tier) and vertical (quality/price tiers).

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: When a superior new product meets NO expressed/latent need, N. Balasubramanian's principles apply: don't trust market research (unreliable here) — directional accuracy is enough; DE-RISK failure by keeping the initial budget and advertising low-key; EDUCATE channel partners/retailers on the new product's value; use your OWN/unique retail channels if others resist; DON'T ANTAGONISE customers; try unique promotions, free samples and trials to build word of mouth; DEMONSTRATE the product and correct wrong perceptions with value/total-cost comparisons; respond to complaints; persist with consumer trials and keep internal communication consistent; and WAIT for the tipping point — advertise heavily only once the market is ready (advertising prematurely makes customers reject the product). Cases: Safal frozen vegetables, Real Good Chicken, Tropicana, Pedigree pet food.

distractors.wrong: With no latent demand you should spend heavily on advertising upfront
distractors.why: advertise only at the tipping point when the market is ready; premature advertising makes customers reject it

distractors.wrong: Market research reliably guides a no-latent-need launch
distractors.why: research is unreliable here; rely on directional accuracy, trials, demonstration and word of mouth

nodes.sample_question: What principles guide creating demand for a product with no latent need (per Balasubramanian)? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Front-loading advertising and trusting market research when the market isn't ready.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A new product can leverage RESOURCES (existing vs new) for USERS (existing vs new), giving a 2x2 of risk/cost: (1) existing resources -> existing users: leverage to create new value for current customers — LOW cost, LOW risk (best first); (2) NEW resources -> existing users: add features/offerings to the current base — higher cost, low risk; (3) existing resources -> NEW users: leverage current resources for new users — low cost, higher risk; (4) NEW resources -> NEW users: new value propositions for new users — HIGH cost, HIGH risk (last resort, after exhausting the other three). Avoid conflict with well-selling existing products.

distractors.wrong: Targeting new users with new resources is the safest first move
distractors.why: that quadrant is HIGH cost/HIGH risk and a last resort; start with existing resources for existing users

distractors.wrong: All four quadrants carry the same risk
distractors.why: risk/cost rise as you move from existing-existing (low/low) to new-new (high/high)

nodes.sample_question: Draw the resources x users 2x2 for product options and rank the quadrants by risk/cost. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Jumping to the new-resources/new-users quadrant instead of exhausting safer options first.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Five IP types protect new products: (1) UTILITY PATENT — temporary government monopoly on a useful, novel, non-obvious idea (e.g. significant new software); (2) DESIGN PATENT — protects a design resulting from high skill/effort (need not be novel/non-obvious); (3) COPYRIGHT — exclusive right over an original creation in tangible expression; need NOT be registered/filed (burden falls on the copier to prove independence); (4) TRADEMARK — exclusive government-granted right to a name/symbol (revocable); (5) TRADE SECRET — protection by SECRECY, not registration (Coke/Pepsi formula). A patent holder can exclude others from using/selling/importing the infringing product and sue infringers; firms also BARTER patents as a negotiating tool (more patents = more bargaining power).

distractors.wrong: Copyright must be registered/filed to be valid
distractors.why: copyright exists on original tangible expression WITHOUT registration; the burden shifts to the copier

distractors.wrong: A trade secret is a type of patent
distractors.why: a trade secret is protected by SECRECY, not by any government patent grant or registration

nodes.sample_question: Name the five types of intellectual property and how each is protected. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing copyright (no registration) and trade secret (secrecy) with registered patents/trademarks.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Patenting is expensive and slow, so plan it: file within one year of first disclosure (a PROVISIONAL patent can delay full filing while refining the idea), use multi-country filing and a known patent attorney; some firms file a cheaper provisional rather than a full patent. Patents act like a FENCE/wall of related patents signalling territory to deter imitation — but they are imitation BARRIERS, not guaranteed market monopoly, and litigation is hard to pursue. Strategy elements: establish rights, license, enforce against infringers, defend property rights in court, and LEVERAGE patents to bargain or generate licensing rents; large firms (IBM, Intel, Microsoft) acquire firms for important patents rather than reinventing.

distractors.wrong: A patent guarantees a market monopoly
distractors.why: patents are imitation barriers, not guaranteed monopolies; many cover minor tweaks and litigation is hard

distractors.wrong: You should file a full patent on the final product only, never earlier
distractors.why: firms file PROVISIONAL patents early (within a year of disclosure) to mark territory while refining the idea

nodes.sample_question: What is patent strategy, and why is a patent not a guaranteed monopoly? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Overstating patents as monopolies and missing the provisional-filing/licensing/deterrent strategy.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Raw ideas are unproven/unsellable, so file a local provisional patent then build/test the product. Handle DESIGN piracy by PRODUCT ENHANCEMENT (redesign into higher-value products for upper-class niche customers who prefer originals over fakes) and SERVICE ENHANCEMENT (bundle skilled services/AMCs that lock in customers); litigation is hard to pursue. Handle DIGITAL piracy: legislation exists but is weakly enforced, so use ENCRYPTION/DRM, license control, forensic WATERMARKING, tokenised/multi-factor authentication, content delivery networks, automated web-crawling takedowns, and blockchain. Or undercut piracy with LOW price points (Apple 99-cent songs, Moser Baer 3-movie DVDs at ~50 cents) so copying is unviable; keep frequent updates/patches; large firms use lawyers as a deterrent.

distractors.wrong: Litigation is the most effective remedy against piracy
distractors.why: litigation is hard/slow; product/service enhancement, encryption, watermarking and low pricing are the practical remedies

distractors.wrong: Raising price defeats piracy
distractors.why: a LOW price point makes piracy unviable (99-cent songs); a high price widens the gap pirates exploit

nodes.sample_question: How can firms deal with design piracy and digital piracy respectively? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Relying on litigation instead of enhancement, technical protection and low-price deterrence.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: CarryPro (founder Ankit Agarwal, a travel blogger with product-management experience, 2017-18) is a late entrant to a competitive Indian backpack market (Wildcraft, Decathlon/Quechua, Thule). The founder spotted a gap (bulky, poorly-organised travel bags) — a classic product-manager/effectuation move (start from the user's problem). Three focused products avoid cannibalisation by USE-CASE segmentation: HOBO40 (3-5 day travel, best-selling, less competition), HOBO25 (daily/office/gym, most competition), PANGO (camera/creators, highest revenue, uncontested niche). Distribution is OMNICHANNEL (Amazon/Myntra/website + pop-ups/B2B/specialty retail). Strengths: high-quality materials (YKK zips), affordable-premium pricing matching competitors with extra features. Weakness: low brand awareness/recall. Key dilemmas: (a) reasonable price vs reposition premium (don't cut Pango's price — price signals quality; consider a separate sub-brand instead); (b) selective (premium image, limited reach) vs intensive (visibility, dilutes brand) distribution.

distractors.wrong: CarryPro should cut Pango's price to attract beginners
distractors.why: price signals quality; the recommendation is to keep price and, if needed, launch a separate lower-feature sub-brand

distractors.wrong: CarryPro's three products overlap and cannibalise each other
distractors.why: they are segmented by USE CASE (travel/daily/camera) with distinct sizes, avoiding cannibalisation

nodes.sample_question: How did CarryPro use use-case segmentation, and what are its two key strategic dilemmas? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Recommending a price cut that erodes quality signal, or seeing the three products as overlapping.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A strategy canvas is a VISUAL plot of the levels of investment in the key competitive factors of an industry, used to picture the existing industry and design a different model. Southwest Airlines example: plotted against full-service carriers on factors (price, meals, lounge, seat selection, hub connectivity), Southwest scores LOW on most and HIGH on speed/punctuality, operating point-to-point between smaller (tier-2) airports with a single aircraft type — effectively competing with cars/buses, not just airlines. The canvas reveals where to operate differently from the industry 'value curve'.

distractors.wrong: A strategy canvas plots market share over time
distractors.why: it plots the LEVEL of investment in competitive factors (the value curve), not market share over time

distractors.wrong: Southwest competed head-on with full-service airlines on the same factors
distractors.why: Southwest scored low on most industry factors and high on speed/point-to-point, competing more with cars/buses

nodes.sample_question: What does a strategy canvas plot, and how did Southwest's value curve differ from rivals'? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reading the canvas as a share/time chart rather than a competitive-factor value curve.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The ERRC grid builds a blue-ocean value curve by asking four questions: ELIMINATE which factors the industry takes for granted? (e.g. free meals, lounge for price-sensitive flyers); REDUCE which factors below the industry standard? (e.g. number of connecting options); RAISE which factors above the industry standard? (e.g. punctuality, turnaround/service); CREATE which factors the industry never offered? (e.g. point-to-point tier-2-to-tier-2 routes / a new market). Eliminate+Reduce lower cost; Raise+Create lift buyer value — together breaking the usual value-cost trade-off.

distractors.wrong: ERRC stands for Expand, Refine, Reduce, Compete
distractors.why: ERRC = Eliminate, Reduce, Raise, Create — the four blue-ocean actions

distractors.wrong: Eliminating and reducing factors lowers buyer value
distractors.why: Eliminate/Reduce lower COST; Raise/Create lift buyer VALUE — together they break the value-cost trade-off

nodes.sample_question: Name the four actions in the ERRC grid and which lower cost vs raise value. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Misnaming ERRC or assigning eliminate/reduce to value rather than cost.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: RED ocean strategy competes in EXISTING market space for the same customers — beating rivals in a zero-sum, often price-warring contest (a 5th restaurant on a street of 4). BLUE ocean strategy creates UNCONTESTED market space where competition is irrelevant, serving non-customers with something different and capturing NEW demand. Red ocean exploits existing demand and accepts the value-cost trade-off (differentiation OR low cost); blue ocean breaks the trade-off (pursues differentiation AND low cost). Steps: draw the current strategic canvas, study the field, apply ERRC, deliver within capacity, and craft a compelling tagline.

distractors.wrong: Blue ocean strategy means out-competing rivals on price in the existing market
distractors.why: that is RED ocean; blue ocean creates uncontested space and makes competition irrelevant

distractors.wrong: Blue ocean still requires a value-cost trade-off
distractors.why: blue ocean BREAKS the trade-off, pursuing differentiation AND low cost simultaneously

nodes.sample_question: Contrast red and blue ocean strategy on competition, demand and the value-cost trade-off. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating blue ocean as merely winning the existing-market price war.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: IPL is a blue-ocean product: it solved test/ODI cricket's drawbacks (too long, boring for youth, empty stadiums) by creating a short T20 format, city FRANCHISE model (local connect), player AUCTION (market-driven salaries, balanced teams), iconic players, prime-time evening + summer-vacation slots, and a stadium ENTERTAINMENT package (music, cheerleaders, Bollywood owners) — borrowing from EPL/NBA and timed to the 2007 T20 World Cup win. It added new, non-cricket customers (city affiliation, entertainment). The iPhone is also blue-ocean: it eliminated the fixed keyboard, added finger-touch and real internet use, creating the smartphone market. Blue oceans don't stay blue — competitors copy and new models emerge.

distractors.wrong: IPL simply shortened the existing cricket format
distractors.why: IPL created a new product: franchise + auction + entertainment + timing, attracting NON-cricket customers — a blue ocean

distractors.wrong: Blue oceans remain uncontested permanently
distractors.why: competitors copy successful blue oceans; they turn red over time and new models must emerge

nodes.sample_question: Explain why the IPL is considered a blue-ocean product. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Seeing IPL/iPhone as mere format/feature tweaks rather than new-market creation.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: An effective new-product business plan: opens with a clear, FACT-BASED executive summary; justifies the new BUSINESS MODEL (the gap/unmet need it solves); shows how to REACH and CONVERT buyers; identifies an implementation plan and required support/stakeholders; covers RISKS and mitigations (plan B/C); shows fit with the firm's business GOALS/core competence; and presents a few CRITICAL numbers (not a full DPR) that build the team's credibility by pre-empting obvious questions. Typical MISTAKES: customer-side (shallow customer understanding, choosing convenient over best-fit markets, me-too vs value creation, wrong segment, ignoring customer-view quality, too few price options, underpricing vs value-based pricing) and cost-side (excessive startup capital/buying vs renting, too much space, wasteful resources, high fixed salaries, paid ads before the market is ready, high fixed/low variable cost without cost-volume-profit analysis).

distractors.wrong: A business plan should be an exhaustive detailed project report
distractors.why: it presents a few CRITICAL numbers and answers obvious questions to build credibility — not a full DPR

distractors.wrong: Underpricing is a safe way to win customers
distractors.why: underpricing loses margin; use value-based pricing tied to willingness to pay — underpricing is a listed mistake

nodes.sample_question: List the components of an effective new-product business plan and two common mistakes. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Drowning the plan in detail and underpricing instead of value-based pricing.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Firms hire strategy consultants for new products when there is an UNDIAGNOSED performance problem, a KNOWN problem they can't fix, or a difficult strategic CHOICE/trade-off. Clients rely on consultants for: domain EXPERTISE; ability to SYNTHESISE relevant data from many sources; an objective outsider VIEW; CREATING new options; STRUCTURING strategic choices and identifying/demonstrating the best option (cost-benefit); and helping IMPLEMENT and show early results. Roles span early (proposal/problem identification, hypothesis building, pre-consulting scoping) through post-sign-off (research, scenario/sensitivity analysis, recommendations, quick-win prototype tests). In larger firms the NPD role is limited to where specific expertise is needed.

distractors.wrong: Consultants are hired only when a firm already knows the exact problem
distractors.why: they are also hired for UNDIAGNOSED problems and difficult strategic choices, not just known ones

distractors.wrong: Consultants only diagnose and never implement
distractors.why: they also help implement the chosen option and demonstrate early results/quick wins

nodes.sample_question: When do firms need strategy consultants for new products, and what do clients rely on them for? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Limiting consultants to diagnosis and ignoring option-creation and implementation roles.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: An 'appropriate' product for an emerging market meets customer needs BETTER than competition, with better user-defined quality, unique benefits, solves real problems, reduces in-use cost over the lifetime, and has visible benefits (novelty is a bonus, not the main driver). FAILURE: AMD's Personal Internet Communicator (PIC, 2004, ~$250) — robust, award-winning design but failed (divested 2006) because it competed against cheap cyber-cafes and second-hand PCs, with high recurring internet-subscription cost and added technology risk. SUCCESS: Nokia 3310/3315 and 1100 — lowest price, robust, long battery, reliable, good resale, no non-essential features, simple interface, large fonts (for first-time/senior/semi-literate users); the 1100 added a torchlight, cleanable surface, grip lines and a clear red on/off button from rural field study. Lesson: fewer, well-fitted features beat feature-rich, award-winning products that ignore market context.

distractors.wrong: AMD's PIC failed because of poor design
distractors.why: it WON design awards; it failed on market fit — cheap cyber-cafes/second-hand PCs and high recurring cost

distractors.wrong: More features make a product more appropriate for emerging markets
distractors.why: fewer, well-fitted features (Nokia 1100 torchlight, simple interface) beat feature-rich misfits

nodes.sample_question: Contrast AMD's PIC failure with Nokia's success to explain what makes a product 'appropriate' for an emerging market. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Crediting design awards/feature count over real market-fit and in-use cost.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Designing for emerging markets means adjusting frameworks to local conditions: customers are VALUE-sensitive (not merely price-sensitive) — they want adequate quality at a fair price (the middle/sweet spot, not the cheapest nor ultra-premium); poor INFRASTRUCTURE (traffic/roads -> need nearby stores and home delivery; unstable electricity -> battery/no-power products like Pureit/Tata Swach water filters; low internet bandwidth -> low-bandwidth design); cheap LABOUR (less need to automate; last-mile via people); limited REAL ESTATE (smaller homes -> smaller products); and social/cultural differences (community vs individualistic living -> marketing that lets buyers seek others' opinions/likes). Minimalist/limited design has a strong use case (few menu items, few mutual funds — e.g. Parag Parikh Flexi Cap).

distractors.wrong: Emerging-market customers are simply price-sensitive (want the cheapest)
distractors.why: they are VALUE-sensitive: adequate quality at a fair price — the middle sweet spot, not the cheapest

distractors.wrong: Western product designs transfer unchanged to emerging markets
distractors.why: concepts need adjustment to local infrastructure, labour, real-estate and cultural conditions

nodes.sample_question: List the key characteristics of emerging markets that shape new product design. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating value-sensitivity with cheapness and ignoring infrastructure/cultural constraints.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: For base-of-pyramid (bottom-of-pyramid) markets: build FUNCTIONAL, minimal-feature products (avoid confusing extras); make them INTUITIVE (little training, dealer can demo); demonstrate utility easily; make them ROBUST to harsh conditions/misuse; allow easy low-risk TRIAL (modular series bought in steps); finance INNOVATIVELY to match cash flows (loans/EMI/subscription); SUPPORT the whole product life (long warranty, spares, service, easy upgrade/exchange with high trade-in value); and keep tight CONTROL of the price-performance equation, communicating VALUE. Six new business OPTIONS map intent x affordability: (1) high intent + can afford high price; (2) high intent + can afford higher-feature price; (3) high demand -> move users to appropriately-designed products; (4) latent demand, users think it too high-priced; (5) latent demand, users think it too cheap (e.g. Zudio positions higher to avoid the 'too cheap' stigma); (6) high demand -> aggressively reach out with a better product. Customers are value-sensitive, wanting BOTH quality and low price.

distractors.wrong: BoP customers want the absolute cheapest regardless of quality
distractors.why: they are value-sensitive and want BOTH reasonable quality and low price; control the price-performance equation

distractors.wrong: A 'too cheap' price always helps in BoP markets
distractors.why: a too-cheap signal can imply low quality (latent-demand option 5); brands like Zudio position higher to avoid the stigma

nodes.sample_question: What design principles and business options apply when building base-of-pyramid markets? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Designing the cheapest possible product and ignoring the 'too cheap = low quality' perception.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Design thinking starts from understanding the USER/problem and combines LEFT-brain (linear, logical, sequential, structured) with RIGHT-brain (design synthesis, context, pattern, artistic) thinking (Dan Pink): the right-brain abilities — DESIGN, STORY, SYMPHONY (big-picture/strategic), EMPATHY, PLAYFULNESS, and MEANING — are increasingly valued because analytics is being automated. The DESIGN THINKING CYCLE is user-based, problem-solving, iterative: understand users -> rapid experimentation -> user-led feedback -> prototype cycles, staying flexible and open. The 4D framework (UK Design Council): DISCOVER (understand daily experiences/causal influences) -> DEFINE (clear opportunity) -> DEVELOP (rapid idea testing/feedback/business model) -> DELIVER (measure impact, prove the concept with real users). Design itself = creative organising of human, physical and technical knowledge toward functional/aesthetic/ergonomic/economic goals under constraints, aligned with the firm's vision/values.

distractors.wrong: Design thinking is a purely linear, logical (left-brain) process
distractors.why: it combines left-brain logic with right-brain design/empathy/story and is iterative, not linear

distractors.wrong: The 4D framework is Discover, Decide, Demo, Deploy
distractors.why: it is Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver (UK Design Council)

nodes.sample_question: What right-brain abilities does design thinking emphasise, and name the four stages of the 4D framework. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating design thinking as linear left-brain analysis or misnaming the 4D stages.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Soft innovation (Stoneman) creates product VARIETIES of aesthetic/intellectual/intangible appeal rather than functional performance — book titles, packaging, marketing/ads, music/food creations, new delivery methods, smell/touch/colour, and price variations (mobile tariff/combo offers). High product variety/distinctiveness commands higher premiums/profits; it is protected by DESIGN REGISTRATION, not patents, and the commodity demand-supply logic doesn't apply (it adds options rather than shifting demand-supply). It relates to HYPER-COMPETITION (new products launched at high frequency, where NOT launching risks losing share even though launching is costly/risky): EPISODIC hyper-competition gives temporary gains (fancy packaging, dies out soon) while TRANSFORMATIONAL hyper-competition reflects major, likely-permanent shifts in tastes/technology (feature phone -> smartphone; health consciousness) and leads to a POST-hyper-competition era with new bases of competition (few players die, more persist).

distractors.wrong: Soft innovation changes a product's functional performance
distractors.why: soft innovation changes aesthetic/intangible appeal and variety, NOT functional performance

distractors.wrong: Soft innovation is protected by patents
distractors.why: it is protected by DESIGN REGISTRATION, not patents; commodity demand-supply logic doesn't apply

nodes.sample_question: Define soft innovation and distinguish episodic from transformational hyper-competition. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing soft (aesthetic/intangible) innovation with functional innovation, or episodic vs transformational hyper-competition.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Luxottica (Italian eyewear MNC, founded 1961) achieved near-monopoly power via VERTICAL INTEGRATION across the value chain: it bought distribution companies, signed LICENSING agreements to make frames for luxury brands (Armani 1988, then Chanel, Prada, Versace, Burberry, etc.), owns its own brands (Ray-Ban, Oakley, Persol), acquired the largest lens maker (Essilor, 2018) and major retail chains (LensCrafters, Sunglass Hut, Pearle Vision), and owns a large vision-insurance provider. Owning manufacturing + brands + lenses + retail gives it pricing power with markups reportedly up to ~1000% — possible only because competition is minimal (low hyper-competition), analogous to De Beers in diamonds. Lesson: vertical integration can create a near-monopoly and pricing power in a low-competition industry.

distractors.wrong: Luxottica competes in a hyper-competitive eyewear market
distractors.why: it operates in a LOW-competition, near-monopoly position via vertical integration — the opposite of hyper-competition

distractors.wrong: Luxury brands like Armani manufacture their own eyewear
distractors.why: they license/outsource manufacturing to Luxottica, which holds the pricing power

nodes.sample_question: How did Luxottica use vertical integration to achieve pricing power? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming eyewear is hyper-competitive or that luxury brands make their own frames.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Product launch is the set of MARKETING + technical activities that take the developed product to market; marketing planning must be intense and UPFRONT (and sustained), because once released, control is limited and problems are costly to fix. Weak strategic planning shows up as problems at market; strong upfront planning anticipates problems and prepares plan B/C/D. Distinguish STRATEGIC decisions (long-term, high-impact: platform decisions — whom to sell, how) from TACTICAL decisions (operational, day-to-day: the marketing-mix). Five requirements for an effective launch plan: it is central to the NPD process (don't neglect it), begins EARLY, is based on quality market information gathered through testing, provides adequate human/financial RESOURCES (sales, support, service as part of the team), and REVISITS the PIC strategy/goals at each stage to stay on course (be effective, not just fast).

distractors.wrong: Marketing/launch planning should begin only near the launch date
distractors.why: it begins EARLY in the NPD process and is sustained; weak/late planning shows up as market problems

distractors.wrong: Strategic and tactical launch decisions are the same
distractors.why: strategic = long-term platform decisions (whom/how to sell); tactical = day-to-day marketing-mix execution

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish strategic from tactical launch decisions and list the requirements for an effective launch plan. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Starting launch planning late and conflating strategic platform decisions with tactical mix.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: High-level launch (platform) decisions set tone and direction: TYPE OF DEMAND sought (stimulate PRIMARY demand for a new-to-world product, replacement/migration demand for an upgrade, or SELECTIVE demand for a new line in an established market — e.g. the iPhone 2007 launch creating primary demand); PERMANENCE (is the product meant to stay, stay-if-goals-met, or temporary/seasonal?); AGGRESSIVENESS (aggressive vs cautious vs balanced entry); COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE (cost leader vs differentiation, within a quality-cost-speed triad); product-line REPLACEMENT (cannibalise your own product before competitors do — e.g. Gillette); COMPETITIVE RELATIONSHIP (ignore vs reference competition — e.g. Pepsi vs Coke); SCOPE of market entry (roll out gradually vs full market); and IMAGE (create a new image, major change, or no change — e.g. Maruti's Nexa for premium).

distractors.wrong: Every launch should stimulate the same kind of demand
distractors.why: launches target different demand types: primary (new-to-world), replacement/migration, or selective (new line)

distractors.wrong: Firms should never cannibalise their own products
distractors.why: product-line replacement deliberately cannibalises your own product before competitors do (Gillette's blade ladder)

nodes.sample_question: List the strategic platform decisions a firm makes at launch (e.g. demand type, permanence, aggressiveness). (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating launch as one-size-fits-all and avoiding self-cannibalisation.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Target-market decisions apply marketing fundamentals (segmentation, targeting, positioning, 4Ps) with NPD nuances: segment by END-USE (running vs walking shoes), GEOGRAPHY/DEMOGRAPHY (include/exclude specific segments), BEHAVIOURAL/PSYCHOGRAPHIC (values/lifestyle — e.g. Titan's Mia for working women; traders vs long-term investors), and BENEFIT segmentation (the benefit map vs competitors). Digital enables MICRO-marketing / MASS CUSTOMISATION via four customizer types: COLLABORATIVE (involve the customer early, e.g. Dell.com configuration), ADAPTIVE (customer adapts a standard product), COSMETIC (minimal/surface changes), and TRANSPARENT (customise without the customer's explicit involvement). Made-to-order (Dell, Chipotle/Subway) vs made-to-stock.

distractors.wrong: Mass customisation has a single approach
distractors.why: there are four customizer types: collaborative, adaptive, cosmetic and transparent

distractors.wrong: Cosmetic and collaborative customisation are identical
distractors.why: cosmetic = minimal surface change to a standard product; collaborative = involve the customer early in real customisation (Dell)

nodes.sample_question: Name the four mass-customisation (customizer) types with an example of one. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating mass customisation as one approach instead of four distinct customizer types.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Diffusion describes how a new product spreads. FIVE factors affect adoption SPEED: (1) RELATIVE ADVANTAGE (clear superior value -> faster, e.g. Google's clean superior search); (2) COMPATIBILITY (fits current usage/activity -> faster; deviates -> slower, e.g. microwave); (3) COMPLEXITY (complex -> slower; simple -> faster, e.g. Apple Newton vs iPod); (4) DIVISIBILITY/TRIALABILITY (can be sampled in small portions -> faster; hard for big-ticket items); (5) COMMUNICABILITY/OBSERVABILITY (tangible, observable benefit -> faster; subtle/emotional benefit -> slower). FIVE adopter CATEGORIES over time: INNOVATORS (~first 2.5-5%, experiment for fun), EARLY ADOPTERS (~10-15%), EARLY MAJORITY (~30%, after word of mouth), LATE MAJORITY (wait and watch), LAGGARDS (last, reluctant). New products should initially target innovators + early adopters, not everyone.

distractors.wrong: A new product should target the whole market (all adopter categories) at launch
distractors.why: initially target innovators + early adopters who spread the word; late majority/laggards come later

distractors.wrong: Trialability and observability are the same diffusion factor
distractors.why: trialability/divisibility = can it be sampled in small portions; observability/communicability = is the benefit visible/easy to communicate

nodes.sample_question: List the five factors affecting adoption speed and the five adopter categories. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Targeting everyone at launch and conflating the diffusion factors.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Positioning addresses WHY target buyers should buy your product over others, via its features/benefits — originating in advertising, it is now an ingredient of product strategy and the charter, with brand/price/promotion/distribution all kept CONSISTENT with the position (inconsistency confuses customers and causes failure). The FEATURE-FUNCTION-BENEFIT triad: FEATURE = a product attribute (toothpaste's salt/mint/red colour); FUNCTION = what it does (kills germs, long-lasting foam); BENEFIT = what the customer ultimately feels/gets (confidence, white teeth, fresh breath). Effective positioning communicates the feature, the function it delivers, and the benefit the customer enjoys.

distractors.wrong: A feature and a benefit are the same thing
distractors.why: a feature is a product attribute; a benefit is what the customer feels/gets — the function links them

distractors.wrong: Brand, price and promotion can be positioned independently of the product position
distractors.why: all elements must be CONSISTENT with the position; inconsistency confuses customers and risks failure

nodes.sample_question: Explain the feature-function-benefit triad in positioning with a toothpaste example. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Listing features as if they were benefits and ignoring positioning consistency.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A TRADEMARK is the legally protected identifier (name/symbol/logo, trade-dress like Coke's bottle shape; registration required in developed countries, first-user principle elsewhere). A BRAND is the broader CONCEPT — the feeling, communication and image associated with the trademark, built through product strategy/marketing (not itself legal). Good brand NAMES communicate something about feature/benefit; pitfalls: not anticipating future use, problematic meaning/pronunciation across languages (esp. India/Europe), vague names unrelated to the product, and allocating too little (or, via too many decision-makers, too much) time. BRAND EXTENSION leverages a strong parent brand into new categories (Maggi, Parle, Ashirvaad). STANDARDISE vs ADAPT: keep names consistent globally (Coca-Cola, Gillette) or adapt positioning/names by market (Honda premium in US vs youth/speed in Japan; P&G Tide/Ariel; Unilever Vim/Cif).

distractors.wrong: A brand and a trademark are the same thing
distractors.why: a trademark is the legally protected identifier; a brand is the broader image/feeling/concept built via marketing

distractors.wrong: A strong brand name can be chosen at the last minute
distractors.why: naming needs time and care (future use, cross-language meaning/pronunciation, product relevance); haste is a pitfall

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish a brand from a trademark and list two brand-naming pitfalls. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating brand with trademark and underrating naming/cross-language pitfalls.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Creating a community of diehard fans (Royal Enfield, Harley-Davidson) is a powerful brand strategy and a source of early adopters/ambassadors. SEVEN myths to avoid: (1) a brand community is a marketing strategy — NO, it's a business strategy; (2) it exists to serve the business — NO, it serves PEOPLE (authentic feedback, even negative, builds it); (3) build the brand and the community follows — NO, they develop in PARALLEL and reinforce each other; (4) communities are only for faithful fans — NO, embrace conflicting interests/segments; (5) opinion leaders build communities — NO, everyone plays a role, not just leaders; (6) online social networks are the key tool — NO, use multiple channels aligned to the product (physical adventures for adventure brands); (7) successful communities are tightly managed/controlled — NO, they are democratic and defy managerial control, evolving organically. Strong communities are free, evolving and encouraged without control.

distractors.wrong: A brand community should be tightly managed and controlled by the company
distractors.why: myth: strong communities are democratic and organic; they defy managerial control

distractors.wrong: A brand community exists to serve the business
distractors.why: myth: it serves PEOPLE; authentic (even negative) feedback is what makes it strong

nodes.sample_question: State three myths about brand communities and the reality in each case. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Trying to control/own the community or suppressing negative feedback.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Launch implementation has two phases — PRE-LAUNCH (build capability: training, sales/promotion/advertising, service readiness, stocking at resellers) and the LAUNCH/beachhead stage (marketing expense peaks). Product ANNOUNCEMENT moves through stages: non-disclosure (internal secrecy) -> product testing (beta testers under NDA) -> build ANTICIPATION (buzz, press) -> use INFLUENTIALS (press kits, key customers, influencers, trailers) -> PR/press releases -> launch promotions (full advertising). PRE-ANNOUNCEMENT signals a coming product to hype interest, keep current customers from switching, encourage prospects to WAIT, and BLOCK competitive entry — it works for big-ticket purchases (a buyer will wait months for a car) but not for low-value impulse items. Trade-off: pre-announcing also tips off competition and risks over-hyping; small firms/startups pre-announce eagerly, large firms are circumspect, and highly competitive markets avoid pre-announcing to protect lead time.

distractors.wrong: Pre-announcement works equally well for all products
distractors.why: it works for big-ticket purchases where buyers will wait; not for low-value impulse items

distractors.wrong: Pre-announcement has no downside
distractors.why: it tips off competition (cutting your lead time) and risks over-hyping; large firms are circumspect about it

nodes.sample_question: What is product pre-announcement, what does it aim to do, and when does it work? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Recommending pre-announcement universally and ignoring the competitive-lead-time risk.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: The BEACHHEAD stage (military metaphor) is the launch moment when the product meets the market and its fate is decided — exciting, stressful, and never under ideal conditions (things break; the key is to break inertia and launch, not to wait for perfection; temporary launch marketing becomes permanent). A LEAN LAUNCH stays flexible and minimises time from raw material to consumer: delay decisions, optimise resources, keep the supply chain flexible, don't commit much inventory early, ramp up only as demand confirms (lower lead time, less uncertainty, more operational flexibility — Dell, Benetton). Throughout, keep the ATAR elements in mind: enough advertising (awareness), trial packs/test drives (trial), distribution (availability) and repeat/word-of-mouth.

distractors.wrong: A launch should be delayed until conditions are perfect
distractors.why: conditions are never ideal; break inertia and launch — waiting for perfection is the wrong instinct

distractors.wrong: A lean launch means stocking lots of inventory upfront to be safe
distractors.why: lean launch commits little inventory early and ramps as demand confirms, staying flexible

nodes.sample_question: What is a lean launch and why launch despite imperfect conditions at the beachhead stage? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Over-committing inventory early or waiting for perfect conditions.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Market testing (after the product is largely developed) trades off earlier feedback (cheaper but less accurate) against later feedback (more accurate but costlier). Whether and how to test depends on product TYPE: simple consumer products can be tested early with prototypes/samples and yes/no questions; big-ticket items (cars, appliances) need the near-final product before meaningful testing. Tests cascade: concept test -> product-use test -> marketing-component test (ad copy, pricing, package size). The market test produces a solid forecast for operations/raw-material planning and diagnostic information to revise the product, packaging and the full MARKETING PLAN (target, positioning, price, promotion, distribution, packaging, services). It runs in parallel with product refinement; its output is the final product + final marketing plan.

distractors.wrong: Market testing should always be done as early as possible
distractors.why: timing depends on product type and a cost-vs-accuracy trade-off; big-ticket items need a near-final product

distractors.wrong: Market testing only checks whether people like the product
distractors.why: it produces a solid sales forecast and diagnostics to revise the product, packaging and full marketing plan

nodes.sample_question: What trade-off governs market-testing timing, and what does a market test produce? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Testing too early for products that need a finished form, or ignoring the forecast/plan output.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Three families of market-testing methods by increasing realism/cost: (1) PSEUDO SALE — no real money changes hands: SPECULATIVE sale ('would you buy it if made?', fits B2B/durables with close client relationships) and SIMULATED TEST MARKET (STM) — a false buying situation/simulation parameterising ATAR (awareness, trial, availability, repeat), cheaper/confidential/faster for packaged goods but managers distrust the mathematical output. (2) CONTROLLED SALE — real purchase under controlled conditions: informal selling, direct marketing, and MINI-MARKETS (a few retailers/one chain, e.g. selling only via DMart for clean feedback). (3) FULL SALE — TEST MARKET in representative cities (treatment vs control cities) to fine-tune a national launch; pros: abundant actionable information; cons: expensive, slow, results hard to project to other markets, and competition can spoil it (e.g. drop price/coupons). Pepsi Kona (coffee-cola) failed in its Philippines test market; Pepsi One succeeded by communicating similarity to the core brand.

distractors.wrong: A simulated test market (STM) involves real customer purchases
distractors.why: STM is a PSEUDO sale (simulation, no real money); real purchases occur in controlled-sale and full-sale methods

distractors.wrong: A full test market is cheap and easily projected to other regions
distractors.why: full test markets are expensive, slow and hard to project; competition can also spoil them

nodes.sample_question: Name the three families of market-testing methods and give an example technique in each. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Misclassifying STM as a real sale or assuming test markets are cheap and generalisable.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: A launch management system manages risk in four steps: (1) SPOT potential problems (via situation analysis, role-play/game-theory of competitor responses, concept-test data, and hierarchy-of-effects/what-satisfies-customers); (2) SELECT which to CONTROL — using a likelihood x potential-damage matrix, focus on the high-likelihood/high-damage (devastating) cells, ignore low/low; (3) develop CONTINGENCY plans for the selected control events; (4) design a TRACKING system (trigger points, tracking variables) to detect and respond. Post-launch assessment captures learning (NPD is continuous). INNOVATION METRICS come in three groups: INPUT (R&D spend, employees on innovation, % ideas from outside), PROCESS (new products introduced, time to market, patents filed/commercialised, budget/time/cost vs plan), and PERFORMANCE (total sales revenue, % sales from new products, ROI on innovation, break-even time, customer-satisfaction improvement). Avoid too few metrics (blind) or too many (analysis paralysis).

distractors.wrong: The launch management system focuses on every possible problem equally
distractors.why: it SELECTS high-likelihood/high-damage problems to control via a likelihood x damage matrix; low/low are ignored

distractors.wrong: Input, process and performance metrics measure the same thing
distractors.why: input = R&D spend/people/external ideas; process = time-to-market/patents/plan-vs-actual; performance = sales/ROI/break-even

nodes.sample_question: List the four steps of a launch management system and the three groups of innovation metrics. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Trying to control all problems and conflating input/process/performance metrics.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: When a product fails, options include temporarily pulling it (freeze promotions, fix, re-execute) or investing more — but if convinced it won't work, cut it and redeploy. Product DELETION is a complex, ripple-effecting decision run in four stages: (1) RECOGNITION — compare performance against the initial plan guideposts (market share, growth rate, profit margin, sales revenue) to identify a deletion candidate; (2) ANALYSIS/REVITALISATION — can it be restored? (quality/process/product improvement, new markets, reposition, lower price for a mass/tier-2 market, different geography — e.g. Bajaj bikes in Africa); (3) EVALUATION/DECISION FORMULATION — consider effects on overheads, firm policy, capacity utilisation; (4) IMPLEMENTATION — delete, milk (no investment, run till it lasts, maybe cut price), or SELL the product/technology to another player (startups sell to a larger player).

distractors.wrong: Product deletion is a single, simple decision
distractors.why: it is a complex four-stage process (recognition, analysis/revitalisation, evaluation, implementation) with firm-wide ripple effects

distractors.wrong: A failing product must be scrapped immediately
distractors.why: options include revitalising, repositioning to a new market/geography, milking it, or selling the product/technology

nodes.sample_question: Describe the four stages of the product deletion process. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating deletion as instant scrapping rather than a staged decision with revitalisation/sale options.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Public-policy concerns (environment, health — e.g. Maggi MSG, sugar in baby food, McDonald's obesity suits) can tarnish a firm's image and share price, so product managers must anticipate them. The life cycle has FOUR phases: (1) STIRRING — isolated individuals/activists/NGOs flag an issue that nobody notices (can last years/decades; firms usually ignore it until a mishap); (2) TRIAL SUPPORT — an influential champion/leader takes up the cause, creating visibility and a movement (the firm can still defuse it, or it dies down); (3) POLITICAL ARENA — the cause reaches political visibility, policy debates and possible legislation (the firm faces legal/regulatory battle, may settle or fight); (4) REGULATORY ADJUSTMENT — laws are passed then refined; firms exploit interpretation/loopholes during the 'jockeying' period until laws become precise (e.g. Nestle baby-food advertising bans). The firm can de-escalate (back to idleness) or it escalates upward.

distractors.wrong: Public-policy issues appear suddenly with no warning
distractors.why: they pass through stirring -> trial support -> political arena -> regulatory adjustment; early signals exist for years

distractors.wrong: Once an issue reaches the political arena the firm can still easily close it down
distractors.why: by the political-arena phase it is hard to defuse; the firm faces legal/regulatory battle, settlement or fight

nodes.sample_question: Describe the four phases of the public-policy issue life cycle. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating policy crises as sudden and missing the early stirring-phase signals.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Product liability holds manufacturers, service providers and sellers responsible for harm from DEFECTIVE products; in India the Consumer Protection Act (CPA) empowers consumers, and developed markets have stricter laws. Consumers can claim compensation for personal injury, property damage or death from manufacturing defects, design flaws, poor quality or inadequate warnings — at any stage from buying to using. Liability mainly applies to GOODS (physical harm), less to services. Because an injured individual 'has nothing to lose' while escalation/media damage the firm, companies often SETTLE out of court. To manage it, give adequate CAUTION/WARNINGS and highlight misuse (e.g. 'not a flotation device', 'do not eat the rock-garden rocks').

distractors.wrong: Product liability applies mainly to services
distractors.why: it applies mainly to GOODS (physical harm/injury); services carry less physical-harm liability

distractors.wrong: Firms always fight liability suits in court
distractors.why: firms often SETTLE out of court to avoid negative publicity, since the injured individual has little to lose

nodes.sample_question: What is product liability, what can consumers claim for, and how do firms typically manage it? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming liability targets services or that firms always litigate rather than settle.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.concept: Legal bases for liability & product recall
nodes.teaching_note: Four legal bases for product liability (escalating): (1) NEGLIGENCE — the firm was careless (act of commission/omission), e.g. an unsecured wheel; (2) WARRANTY — breach of a promise about features/safety (EXPRESS = stated; IMPLIED = inherent/understood); negligence need not be proven; (3) STRICT LIABILITY — the seller is responsible for not putting a defective product on the market and can be sued even without negligence or a direct sale (e.g. a mobile battery that catches fire); defences include assumption of risk, unforeseeable misuse, and natural acts; (4) MISREPRESENTATION — the product is presented as safe/standard-meeting when it isn't (e.g. a helmet shown protecting a rider but not meeting safety standards). To pre-empt liability, firms do PRODUCT RECALLS: designate a single recall coordinator, ensure clear consumer/intermediary communication, assess risk and take corrective action, recall the whole product line if needed, monitor recall effectiveness, and restore reputation (J&J Tylenol tamper-proof bottles; P&G pet-food full-page recall ads).

distractors.wrong: Strict liability requires proving the firm was negligent
distractors.why: strict liability applies WITHOUT proof of negligence — even without a direct sale, the manufacturer can be liable

distractors.wrong: Express and implied warranties are the same
distractors.why: express = a stated promise; implied = an inherent/understood promise; breach of either creates liability

nodes.sample_question: Name the four legal bases for product liability and outline good recall practice. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the four bases (esp. strict liability needing no negligence) and mishandling recalls.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Environmental issues are a major public-policy area: a product may use scarce/depleting raw materials, cause pollution/excess power-water use in design or manufacture, or be hard to dispose/recycle (plastic). Firms must act socially responsible with SUSTAINABLE DESIGN that reduces negative environmental impact (not optional — it affects reputation). Five strategies to promote sustainable design: (1) innovate at the SYSTEM level (whole product, not just a part); (2) use NEW/less-polluting MATERIALS; (3) invest in NEW TECHNOLOGIES that solve environmental challenges (e.g. LED replacing bulbs); (4) develop new BUSINESS MODELS (sharing/renting cars to cut carbon footprint); (5) help RESTORE the environment. Sustainability has a cost that pressures profit, so firms must think beyond routine models.

distractors.wrong: Sustainable design only means using recycled packaging
distractors.why: it spans five strategies: system-level innovation, new materials, new technologies, new business models, and restoration

distractors.wrong: Sustainable design is cost-free
distractors.why: sustainability carries a cost that pressures profit; firms must consciously think beyond routine models

nodes.sample_question: List the five strategies for promoting sustainable design. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing sustainability to packaging and ignoring its cost/profit tension.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Ethical dilemmas arise across the NPD life cycle, often driven by COST pressure (sustainable/ethical choices cost more): covert/intrusive observation of users (including children) WITHOUT consent during ideation; hiding from distributors/customers that a product is temporary (information concealment); LD50 (lethal-dose-50%) animal testing of chemical products; and off-label marketing of a drug for unapproved uses. Ethics can't be eliminated to a zero-defect ideal, so set REASONABLE goals and a clear GUIDING PRINCIPLE (a fair red/green-flag line) with substantial disclosure. Product managers should: identify ethical issues at the strategy/policy level, maintain ethical standards at reasonable cost, keep internal CONTROL mechanisms so teams follow standards, and educate customers (clear labels, less-sugar/trans-fat products). (Example: GM's hybrid/hydrogen-vehicle willingness-to-pay gap — customers would pay only ~$1,000 premium.)

distractors.wrong: Ethical issues in NPD can be eliminated entirely to a zero-defect standard
distractors.why: they can't be fully eliminated; set reasonable goals and a clear guiding principle with disclosure

distractors.wrong: Ethics is purely an individual matter unrelated to product management
distractors.why: product managers must address ethics at the strategy/policy level and keep control mechanisms, not leave it to individuals

nodes.sample_question: Give two ethical dilemmas in NPD and how a product manager should address ethics. (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Expecting ethics to be perfectly eliminated rather than managed with principles and controls.

nodes.subject: NPD
nodes.teaching_note: Practitioner interviews (Sameer Sawarkar, co-founder of Neurosynaptic Communications, rural tele-healthcare) reinforce core NPD lessons in practice: the initial naive idea (connect a medical device to IIT-built rural kiosks) worked technically but failed because the surrounding ECOSYSTEM was missing (no pharmacy, labs, referral) — technology alone is not the product; the venture was AHEAD OF THE MARKET (~16-17 years), illustrating latent/no-latent demand and the decision to persist (switch to the development/NGO sector) vs abandon; the business model was an AGGREGATOR connecting rural patients to urban doctors via a local entrepreneur-operator; products became CONNECTED DEVICES (recording usage) to prevent misuse/quackery; and disruption came from redesigning PROCESSES, not just technology (Christensen). Lessons: leverage the existing ecosystem, design for real local constraints (power, connectivity, fear of shocks), and that fit/ecosystem and process matter as much as the device.

distractors.wrong: A working technology is automatically a successful product
distractors.why: the device worked technically but failed without the ecosystem (pharmacy/labs/referral); fit and ecosystem matter

distractors.wrong: Being far ahead of the market guarantees success
distractors.why: being ~16-17 years ahead meant no ready market; the team had to persist and switch sectors, not just rely on the tech

nodes.sample_question: What NPD lessons does the Neurosynaptic rural-healthcare journey illustrate about ecosystem and timing? (5M)
nodes.failure_mode: Crediting the technology alone and ignoring ecosystem-fit and market-readiness.
